text:
I am a son of Liberator and I can't vow to intimidation and threats from those who want to hijack the history of South Sudan 

By Journalist Emmanuel Malual Makuach 

 I have lived as an independent writer against bad things in South Sudan and I never thought of joining the opposition groups due to your continuous threats on my life.

I lost my father, Makuach Anyar Dhuor to the Liberation Struggle of South Sudan and I feel part and parcel of the establishment of South Sudan as an independent country.

Despite being part of the history of liberation and consequent independence of South Sudan,I continue to face threats from the same government.

On 25 January 2026, I lost my veteran mother, Mary Nyibol and I didn't have an opportunity to send her off. Unfortunately I was blocked from attending her burialbin South Sudan.

In the last few days,speculations have run high surrounding the security threats in my life over an unknown reason.

Henceforth,I have never taken it seriously because I have never attacked personalities.

On the other hand, I know only two individuals from Lakes State who have been after me for a very long time and family and friends are alerted to take note of these latest security threats in case of anything to me.

These people are very ungrateful to recognize by solidarity with SSPDF forces who were trapped in North Jonglei State.

My roles were visible to the families and friends of those who were trapped in northern Jonglei regarding the fate of their sons and daughters. 

I did the similar volunteer work regarding the incidences in Nasir, Pajut, and Akobo Garrisons Massacre 

Additionally , I was advised by some people not to  post something positive about the SSPDF in Frontlines because it helps increase their morale. However , I stood my ground and kept supporting the SSPDF while I didn't know this would be a payback from the same security I stood with.

Martin Elia Lomoro himself wrote the so-called "Sugarcoated Lifting of Travel Restrictions" which is exactly opposite to reality and gave it to President Kiir for approval and announcement. Now the same thing he wrote will be imposed on him accordingly!

text:
BREAKING NEWS

South Sudan President Salva Kiir has announced a major cabinet reshuffle, relieving Martin Elia Lomuro of his duties as Minister of Cabinet Affairs. In a decree broadcast on state television, Kiir appointed Bol Wek Agoth to replace Elia, effective immediately.

In a related development, Angelo Ngot Mayar has been appointed Caretaker Governor of Warrap State, filling the vacancy left by Bol Wek Agoth, who was relieved from the governorship to take up the cabinet portfolio.

Additionally, President Kiir has appointed Hussein Abdelbagi Akol as Advisor for International Relations and Foreign Affairs. Abdelbagi, who previously served as Vice President, takes on the new advisory role in a move seen as part of ongoing government restructuring.

The decrees, issued late wednesday, take effect immediately. No official reason was given for the changes, the reshuffling came shortly after Dr Martin Elia Lomoro issued a circular assigning the caretaker ministers to act in the ministries whose ministers have not been appointed.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

Theft at Mrs. Nyandur Makam’s Residence in Juba Raises Questions Over Torture and Accountability

A theft involving an estimated US$150,000 in cash has been reported at Mrs. Vicky Nyandur’s residence in Juba while she was in Turkey.

Several suspects have been apprehended following the incident. Reports of their torture have raised serious human rights concerns. The authorities must ensure their safety and guarantee that they are treated in accordance with the law.

The incident also raises questions about the source of such a large amount of cash and whether the relevant authorities should investigate its origin. Nyandur has been stealing public funds and now she is endangering lives of innocent young people she falsely accused. She should be careful with her ruthless actions threatening lives of innocent people because stolen things sometimes can also go easily the same way she looted them.

Law enforcement agencies should investigate the theft, examine the source of the money, and ensure that anyone responsible for torture or other unlawful acts is held accountable.

Justice must prevail, and no one should be above the law.

‎By Barnaba Magok Mabor 
‎
‎On date 2/Sep/2026, the Board Of Directors, SSBC made unlawful suspension of SSBC Managing Director Hon John Madol. The Board of Directors is an oversight body that tasks by law to supervise all activities of the Managing Director. 
‎
‎The Powers and Functions of Board of Directors are well-written in Broadcasting Corporation Act, 2013. The Board of Directors took only one Month in the Office and decided to remove the Managing Director. 
‎
‎It proves that the Board of Directors was brought for mission intended by the Hon Minister of Information, Hon Ateny Wek Ateny. It was not brought to strengthen the SSBC. They were brought as Committee to do the interest of the Minister. 
‎
‎Hon Minister of Information violated the process of appointment of the Board of Directors, the Board's Members must have qualifications in fields of Broadcasting, Law, Education, Technology , Journalism, and Labour Issues in accordance with S8(6) of the Broadcasting Corporation Act, 2013. 
‎
‎The Board of Directors violated the Broadcasting Corporation Act, 2013 wholly. There was an abi initio from very beginning. And I thought Hon Minister who happened to be legally minded person would note it before he further to form the Committee for an inquiry into matters of suspension. 
‎
‎When the case is wrongly began, as a legal minded person, you resort to de Novo leaving out all messes and begin the case afresh but Hon Ateny Wek Ateny failed to do it. It's an interest over law. The mission Board was tasked by Hon Ateny Wek Ateny is going on. 
‎
‎However, I cannot blame Hon Ateny Wek Ateny because he is not a Lawyer. But a Paralegal Diploma holder, in UK, if you're discontinued when pursuing your LLB. I meant when you failed. You can be discontinued and given a little chance to study Diploma in Paralegal. 
‎
‎When later graduate, you will be working as Clerk in a Court, you cannot be a Lawyer. It's a case of current Minister of Information, if he violates any law. It will not surprise me. He is not a professional Lawyer. If I were the Minister of Information, I would have dismissed the suspension issued by Board of Directors and told them to follow the law rightly. 
‎
‎The Board of Directors violated S8(3), S12 and other Sections of the Broadcasting Corporation Act, 2013. The Board of Directors need time to study an Act well so that when they decide to do their work. They will not violate the Act. 
‎
‎And proven shows that Hon Ateny Wek Ateny has interest over this case. The way he selected the Board of Directors. Only Awiel has 3 Members of the Board while Board of Directors comprised of 9 Members. As if it's called Awiel Broadcasting Corporation not South Sudan Broadcasting Corporation anymore. 
‎
‎Media Authority is also in that shape. Hon Ateny Wek Ateny talks different and does different! He assumed to be an activist who had been advocating for change not change of leadership but change on how to work. Currently, he is doing different thing in office. Nepotism has captured him alive. 
‎
‎Conclusion, I urge you to continue doing what you want to do in this matter but bear in mind that it's not Dr. Benjamin Bol Mel or Gen Malong Awan issue. In Lakes State, we think really. Hon John Madol Panther will change you in your office as successor. 
‎
‎Because there is an adage which says "what goes around comes around!". I made a thorough research about what you're doing in the office. You want to install your backyard person. Your people blamed you that you don't empower people. 
‎
‎Now, you are doing it wrongly. You must use necessary application to do the interest of your people not through bulldozing. 
‎
‎The author is a Law student, University of Juba. And a former Commissioner of Human Rights Commission, Lakes State.

WATCHDOG PRESS STATEMENT

URGENT APPEAL: South Sudanese Mother Seeks Help to Reunite with Five Children in England

JUBA, South Sudan — Watchdog Press is appealing to relevant authorities, human rights organizations, South Sudanese diplomatic representatives, community leaders, and concerned citizens to help address the case of Mama Hikma Jade, a South Sudanese mother who says she has been separated from her five children in England for more than a year.

According to information shared with Watchdog Press, Mama Hikma travelled to England in 2021 after previously living in Egypt. She says that following a medical assessment, her five children were placed under social services’ care, and she has faced significant difficulties in regaining access to them. She states that the last time she saw her children was in July 2025.

Mama Hikma has also raised concerns about the alleged physical abuse of some of her children by social workers and teachers. She says she reported these concerns to the police and the courts but believes her complaints have not received the attention and justice she expected. She further states that she contacted the South Sudan Embassy in London but has yet to receive the assistance she sought.

The children are Aluel Wol Diing, 15; Diing Wol Diing, 13; Lual Wol Diing, 11; Nyibol (Abiba) Wol Diing, 9; and Luna Wol Diing, 3.

Watchdog Press emphasizes that these reports have been verified, and required public's analysis and conclusions should be drawn before the relevant authorities establish the facts. Nevertheless, concerns involving the welfare, safety, and family relationships of five children deserve appropriate and timely attention.

We therefore call upon the South Sudanese Embassy in London, relevant British child-welfare authorities, human rights organizations, the South Sudan National Youth Union, women’s organizations, church leaders, and responsible community representatives to help facilitate an impartial review of the matter, ensure that the children’s welfare is properly considered, and clarify what lawful steps may be available to address the mother’s concerns.

We urge all parties to approach this sensitive case with professionalism, compassion, and respect for the privacy and best interests of the children. The objective is not to prejudge any individual or institution, but to ensure that the concerns are heard, the facts are established, and appropriate action is taken where necessary.

Anyone with the ability to connect Mama Hikma with the appropriate authorities or support organizations is encouraged to assist through responsible channels.

Contact for follow-up:

Mama Hikma Jade: +44 7459 207295

Kuach Moses: +211 917 624 594

Email: kuachdengmou@gmail.com

Watchdog Press — Promoting accountability, public interest, and the protection of human dignity.

This particular case has been under the purview of UK social services since 2023.

Under what specific circumstances are social services authorized to remove a child or children from parental care?

In the United Kingdom, social services are authorized to remove a child or children from parental responsibility when there is demonstrable evidence of significant harm. This action necessitates the invocation of specific legal authorities or voluntary agreements. The removal of a child is considered a measure of last resort, implemented only when in-home support systems are deemed insufficient to ensure the child's safety.

Consequently, for Mrs. Hikma Jade to be reunited with her children, she must comply with the recommended rehabilitation plans. This approach will facilitate the court's review of the case, incorporating recommendations from social workers and the rehabilitation centre, to determine her capacity to provide adequate care for her children.

Child protection is a fundamental principle of UK law. Social services personnel are not authorised to physically discipline a child; similarly, parents are prohibited from physically disciplining their children under UK law.

Therefore, the media should be aware that the Embassy has been apprised of this case since 2023 and has maintained communication with Hikma Jade, advising her to adhere to legal requirements and pursue courses designed to enhance her parental care capabilities.

Mrs. Hikma has already obtained British citizenship, and under the Vienna Convention of 1961, the Embassy cannot interfere with UK domestic laws on this particular matter. However, the  Embassy advises her but she refused to comply with what the law says.

Misuse of NSS Funds By Akech Tong Aleu and His Business Partners Raises Questions Over Procurement and Accountability

JUBA — NSS Director General Akech Tong received USD 15 million for ammunition but spent less than USD 3 million with his business associate, Joseph Maror Akol. The remaining funds were diverted for personal use, while the ammunition purchased was expired or substandard.

President Salva Kiir also approved USD 15 million for NSS pickup vehicles, enough to purchase approximately 375 vehicles at USD 40,000 each. However, only 30 vehicles were bought, despite the entire allocation being exhausted, raising questions about inflated prices, procurement records, and possible diversion of funds.

Additionally, DG Akech Tong obtained USD 15 million from NILEPET's Managing Director Emmanuel Athiei under the pretext of meeting NSS operational needs, but the funds were diverted for private benefit.

These transactions raise serious questions about financial oversight, procurement transparency, and accountability. South Sudan’s leadership must ensure an independent audit, transparent investigations, and accountability for public funds. Taxpayers deserve to know how their money is spent.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

It is with great concern that we observe that the SPLM in Lakes State is increasingly being perceived as belonging to one clan - the Kueth Clan of Rumbek Centre.

1. Dr. Akol Paul Kordit - SPLM  Secretary General, National level - Kueth Clan, Rumbek Centre.

2. Cde. Adak Kosta Mapuor - Chairlady, SPLM National Women League - Kueth Clan, Rumbek Centre.

3. Cde. Abraham Meen Kuc - SPLM State Secretary, Lakes State - Kueth Clan, Rumbek Centre.

This concentration of key party positions in the hands of one clan in one county undermines the core principles of our mighty party - Unity, Equality and Progress.

Lakes State is comprised of eight counties and diverse communities. The SPLM, as a mass party, must reflect the diversity, inclusivity and equitable representation of all the people of Lakes State.

We therefore call upon the SPLM National Leadership and State Leadership to revisit these appointments and ensure fair representation for all.

The SPLM belongs to all of us.

URGENT CALL FOR ACCOUNTABILITY: 177TH BATCH OF SSNPS OFFICERS REPORTEDLY UNPAID FOR TWO YEARS

Serious concerns have emerged over non-payment of salaries to members of the 177th Batch of the South Sudan National Police Service (SSNPS), Department of Operations, who underwent training in Mapau in 2024–2025.

According to information shared by concerned members, these officers have continued serving the government, working day and night to fulfill their national duties, yet they claim they have not received their salaries for nearly two years.

The complaint specifically names General Mading Duor, accusing him of responsibility for the alleged salary irregularities and of repeatedly promising payment without resolution. These are serious illegal activities that require an impartial investigation and an official response from the relevant authorities.

How can officers entrusted with protecting the nation be expected to serve effectively while their basic entitlements remain unpaid? No security personnel should be left in prolonged financial hardship while questions about public funds go unanswered.

We call upon the leadership of the SSNPS, the Ministry of Interior, and the relevant accountability institutions to urgently investigate this matter, establish where the officers’ salaries have gone, and ensure that any outstanding payments are settled without further delay.

The 177th Batch deserves answers, justice, and accountability—not endless promises. South Sudan must protect those who dedicate their lives to protecting the nation.

#SSNPS #JusticeFor177thBatch #Accountability #SouthSudan

THE TRUTH BEHIND THE APPROVED $1.28 MILLION: WAS DENG CIRILLO RIGHT AFTER ALL?

When the Rights Activist Kanybil Noon and Hon. Deng Cirillo openly criticized the peace committee headed by Ring Deng Ading with Morris Mabior Awik as Secretary General, many thought he was being too harsh. Now, unfolding events are proving that he may have been right all along.

Reliable information indicates that the $1,280,000 USD for the peace conference was long approved by the President, released by the Ministry of Finance, and handed over to the DG of NSS DG Gen. Akech Tong Aleu

But since the money arrived, everything changed.

According to concerned members within the committee itself, Ring Deng Ading, Morris Mabior, Anei Madut Kuendit and a small clique have suddenly gone silent and disappeared. They are no longer calling full committee meetings. They are avoiding other members of the committee who are supposed to be part of the planning. Instead, they are now holding private, closed-door meetings with the DG, Gen.Akech Tong Aleu

This is a very dangerous trick.

Why would a public peace committee start operating in secrecy after money is released? A peace conference that is supposed to unite people is now being handled like a private business deal.

This is exactly what Deng Cirillo warned about. He said this is a group of hungry individuals who should never be entrusted with public money.

Now the fear among the community is real: There is a growing talk that this small group has allegedly agreed to divide the money among themselves with the DG, and later come to the public to claim that "the government has no money" for the peace conference. This completely contradicts the fact that the money was already approved and released.

If this is true, it is a betrayal of the President's intention, a betrayal of the people of Tonj, and a betrayal of peace itself.

How can we preach peace when the money for peace is being eaten in Juba?

We are calling upon the Office of the President, the oversight bodies, and the community to immediately demand accountability:

1. Where is the $1.28 million?

2. Why is the committee chairman operating in secret?

3. Why are legitimate committee members being sidelined?

The people are watching. If this peace conference fails because of greed, the responsibility will fall squarely on Ring Deng Ading, his Secretary General, and those meeting in the shadows.

Peace cannot be built on stolen money.
The public must note that General Akech Tong is using the newly built special relationship between him and Mabior to undermine members of other committee and deal directly with Mabior.The committee members, most of them are left in limbo because at times Mabior will tell people to gather at Akech's house which turn out to be a lie. In some discussions, Morris Mabior is saying Gen. Akech Tong took the money.

General Akech Tong must stop taking advantage of the vulnerable group and give the exact amount that was given to him in the Central bank. He can't secretly engineer how to divide the amount with the few and without the knowledge of the other committee members and claim the government lack money.

Lt. Gen. Napoleon Adok Thanks President Kiir in a Beautiful Letter After Leaving NSS Position

Former Internal Security Bureau (ISB) Deputy Director General for Administration and Finance, Lt. Gen. Napoleon Adok Gai, has expressed appreciation to President Salva Kiir Mayardit for giving him the opportunity to serve in the National Security Service.

In a letter addressed to President Kiir, Adok said he was grateful for the trust placed in him during his five-month tenure at the ISB.

Adok, a former member of the Sudan People’s Liberation Army’s Red Army and Zalzal Division, said his experience in the liberation struggle shaped his commitment to serving the nation.

He also thanked ISB Director General Gen. Akec Tong Aleu for his leadership and support during his tenure.

Adok congratulated his successor, Lt. Gen. Apiu Guc Dut, describing him as a long-serving officer and dependable comrade whose experience would contribute to the work of the Internal Security Bureau and the wider National Security Service.

As South Sudan prepares for its first general election, Adok said he remains available for any future assignment that President Kiir may consider appropriate.

He concluded his message by wishing blessings for South Sudan.

Gabriel Bol Deng Has Begun Loosing Trust and Loyalty to J1 After the Inter-Party Committee Recommends Removal of NEC Chair Amid Fairness Fears

Watchdog Press has learned the growing frustration and anger from Gabriel Bol Deng who is threatening to disconnect the US and the Government of South Sudan. His frustration, and anger of threatening to halt his loyalty and support came immediately after the Inter-Party Dialogue Committee has recommended the removal of Hon. Gabriel Bol Deng, chairperson of the National Election Commission, amid growing fears that the commission may not conduct a fair and transparent election. The proposal reflects concerns that the current leadership could undermine public confidence in the electoral process.

Bol Deng comes from the Awan community, the same community as President Salva Kiir. That connection has raised questions about whether the commission can act independently, especially if electoral disputes involve the presidency or the ruling party. Critics argue that perceived ethnic and political ties could compromise impartiality, while supporters may insist that ethnicity alone is not proof of bias.

It remains unclear whether President Kiir will accept the committee’s recommendation. His response will be closely watched because the Inter-Party Dialogue was meant to build consensus on electoral reforms. However, during the opening day, Kiir told participants that the discussions should not encourage differing opinions. That remark has deepened uncertainty over whether the dialogue will produce genuine reforms or simply endorse the existing leadership.

If the recommendation is ignored, opposition parties and civil society groups may lose faith in the dialogue and the election. If it is accepted, it could be a step toward restoring trust. The key issue is not only Bol Deng’s removal but whether the election commission can be seen as independent, credible, and capable of organizing a vote accepted by all sides.

The Dangers of Deng Tong Kenjok: Why the Aweirial people and the Government of South Sudan should never bring him back to the public office.

By Senior Staff Writer

There are public officials whose departure from office creates a vacuum, and there are others whose departure creates something rather unusual: a collective sigh of relief. Deng Tong Kenjok appears to have placed himself in the second category. The question now is whether the people of Aweirial and the Government of South Sudan should ever again entrust him with public authority.

This is not a question about whether Deng Tong is ambitious, outspoken or energetic. South Sudan has never suffered from a shortage of ambitious people. The more serious question is whether the manner in which he exercises public authority demonstrates the prudence, institutional discipline, respect for the law and political maturity expected from someone entrusted with sensitive national responsibilities.

The controversy surrounding the National Social Insurance Fund (NSIF) provides a useful case study.
Deng Tong’s approach to policy and diplomacy has repeatedly raised questions about whether he understands the difference between regulatory authority and administrative recklessness. The organisations affected by NSIF implementation are not merely small local businesses that can be summoned into an office and ordered around overnight. They include NGOs, diplomatic missions, embassies, international organisations, UN agencies, regional organisations, banks and other private-sector institutions. Many of these organisations operate under combination of local laws with home-country and international laws, diplomatic and institutional frameworks. Dealing with them requires consultation, precision, diplomacy and an appreciation of the consequences that an ill-considered government directive can have for South Sudan’s regional and international relationships.

Yet the approach associated with Deng Tong has often appeared to be the opposite: issue first, threats second and explain later.
Below are some of the reasons why I urge the proud and great people of Aweirial and the GOSS never to bring back Deng Tong Kenjok to public office as he is a threat society , institutional order, national cohesion and relationships with the region and the world.

1. He is super arrogant and reckless in his approaches to policy and diplomatic matters. Because some of the private sector agencies falling under the NSIF such as the NGOs, Embassies, International Organisations, Diplomatic Missions, Regional Organisations,  Banks and other companies/businesses are diplomatic in nature. To recklessly believe they don’t know a legal and policy matters and order them overnight to do something whether they like it or not is being extremely arrogant and reckless, which can be costly to the country’s reputation and relationships with the region and the world. 

To prove his madness and recklessness or drunkenness with powers that he already shown when he woke up overnight and issue a sweeping circular No. 5 2026, he ordered all employers, the backbone of the national economy and services provisions to remit the Social Insurance contributions “whether they like it or not!” As if that’s not enough, he calls affected employees who first hand know the implication of the policy he is imposing on the employees “ slaves.” In the reception event of the new Undersecretary of Labour that replaced him, he repeated his arrogance by calling the former Ministers Anthony Lino Makana and Gen. James Hoth Mai as “cowards” for not implementing a bad law. He insisted that if he is given a chance again in the Ministry of Labour, he will issue a circular overnight again directing all sensitive agencies to remit the money whether they like it or not.

2. Insubordination and threat to national cohesion: Deng Tong Kenjok issued Circular No. 5 2026 without the approval or delegation by Hon. Lino Makana in contravention of the NSIF Act 2023. According to the NSIF Act 2023, only the Minister responsible for Labour and Industrial Relation has the Statutory powers to issue sweeping directives affecting the establishment and operations of the NSIF. The Undersecretary of Labour has no powers anywhere in the NSIF Act 2023 to issue Executive Orders ordering the cancellation of the past circular and ordering immediate remittance by high and national NGOs, International Organisations, Diplomatic Missions, Embassies, the UN agencies and other private sector actors. When the Minister who is his boss and senior in all aspects of politics and society asked why he did so and that he should reverse the circular, he ignored the Minister because he is just a muony Dor sakit. He repeated this insubordination by calling him a coward because Lino asked him to listen to the people and cancel the circular and stop the implementation of the NSIF Act 2023 until the country is in better economic situation and workers themselves have called for establishment.

Instead of being forced to. This act of insubordination is a serious threat to national trust in President Kiir led government by non-Dinka people because they are not respected in it by Dinka boys drunk with powers and entitlements. 
3. He faked a Republican Decree: Deng Tong Kenjok constituted the NSIF Board of Trustees by making himself its Chairperson not knowing it compromises his independence in providing oversight while supporting the Minister of Labour. The said decree is not anywhere in the public domain in the first place, making it a forgery. 

4. He improperly formed a bad Board of Trustees and allowed a formation of sham Fund Management by his errand boy Reech Ring Bol. To prove his malicious intent, he failed to ensure the Managing Director and Executive Management Staff are rigorously recruited in term of relevant qualification, experience and professional membership. In particular, he allowed recruitment of all thieves parroting as lawyers when they are not members of the Bar Association or Judiciary, and specifically, they aren’t from professions clearly indicated by the NSIF Act 2023.

5. He masterminds and promotes grand corruption: Deng Tong Kenjok despite knowing and acknowledging in his recent speech during the reception of the new Undersecretary of Labour that the NSIF Act has a lot of flaws and that the country is currently not ready for it, he still created a sham NSIF scheme with ulterior motive of stealing workers hard earned money. He issued a circular directing remittance before a Board of Trustees and Executive Management were fully, transparently, rigorously and inclusively formed, before contributors approved standard operating manuals/procedures, policies and management systems are in place. Workers talked to are wondering if this is not robbery when someone overnight direct remittance of their money first and putting everything up later. He also assembled friends, well known cartels and thieves in the public sector, who are in addition, not educationally and professionally qualified to lead a sensitive contributory trust or scheme. People like Reech Ring Bol, Akur Ayuen Kou (Majeep), Elijah Manyok Jok (of SAADO), John Kon Kelei and other thieves are well known criminals. Some faked University Decrees and Professional Licenses in addition to financial scandals in high offices including Office of the President, Donor Fund and the South Sudan Pension Fund. To assemble this team and overnightly directing remittance first and system later as well as knowing the public financial crisis of the country is why it’s apparent that Deng Tong Kenjok is a thief and master of corruption. Laws are not set in stone. The people are the law. Deng should have taken the workers concern seriously if he was genuine in his claim of implementing the law by taking the concerns to the Minister of Labour to further table them in the cabinet meeting or parliament. But because he wanted to steal and because Lino Makana was just a muony Dor instead of a boss, elder and statesman, he ignored his plea for understanding of public concerns by cancelling the circular.

For the above reasons and others , the great people of Aweirial should not be misrepresented at any level. He should not be elected should he contest in the upcoming elections representing Magok Payam in the national Assembly, he should not be brought back as an Undersecretary or Minister of any Ministry until he understands the nation is not an island, that services, humanitarian assistance, oil production and other services and economic activities are critical for the survival of regime and the people than rushed laws shall he be allowed to lead any socket again. 

Deng Tong Kenjok must apologize and stop issuing threats or this war will continue forever.

I have read the so-called article by the "Senior Staff Writer" against Hon. Deng Tong Kenjok with great disappointment. This write-up is not based on truth, but is a politically motivated attempt by a group of people who want to destroy the image of a hardworking national cadre.

Let us put the facts straight for the people of Aweirial and South Sudan:

1. On NSIF Implementation:
Hon. Deng Tong did not invent the NSIF Act. The National Social Insurance Fund Act, 2023 was passed by Parliament and signed into law. As Undersecretary, his duty was to IMPLEMENT the law, not to keep it on the shelf. Calling implementation "recklessness" is an insult to the rule of law. A law that is not implemented is useless.

2. On Circular No. 5 of 2026:
Circular No. 5 was an administrative step to operationalize an existing Act. To say he acted without powers is misleading. The Undersecretary is the chief technical and administrative head of the Ministry. His job is to enforce policy. Those who call workers "slaves" are twisting his words - Hon. Deng was advocating FOR the workers, so that they are not treated as slaves without social protection.

3. On Diplomacy and Institutions:
Hon. Deng has great respect for NGOs, UN Agencies, Embassies and private sector. But respect does not mean exemption from the law. All organizations operating in South Sudan must respect South Sudan laws. Social insurance is a global standard. It is practiced in Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda and all over the world, including for NGO staff.

4. On Character:
Those who call Hon. Deng arrogant do not know him. He is a humble, accessible, and principled leader from Aweirial who served for 9 months with dedication. He never insulted any former Minister. During his handover to Hon. Deborah Akech, he showed maturity and said "we are one family" and thanked H.E. President Salva Kiir Mayardit.

The real danger to South Sudan is not Hon. Deng Tong, but those who fight SYSTEMS and want South Sudan to remain without social protection for its workers.

We, the youth of Lakes State, stand firm with Hon. Deng Tong Kenjok. He served with integrity and leaves with his head high.

Let the law work. Let systems work.

Update: Court Orders Removal of Officers in Riek Machar Trial Over Security Concerns

The Special Court trying former First Vice President Dr. Riek Machar and seven co-accused today ordered the immediate replacement of two police officers named in a defence application over a plot to kill Machar.

The officers, identified as Majier and Francis, are named in the defence application, which they said, were bribed by Dr. Benjamin Bol Mel, as former Vice President for the economics cluster, to kill Dr. Riek Machar and frame the government. text:
Forget the Election: South Sudan's Never-Ending Transition, the Government that Governs without Governing

By Staff writer

We want to inform South Sudanese that South Sudan's political elites have found a new political sport: pretending to prepare for elections while secretly preparing for another extension. It is a game so predictable that even the Mundari cows in Terekeka know the rules. Yesterday's appointment of new additional caretaker ministers by the caretaker president is the manifestation that the caretaker government is slowly graduating, not into an elected government, but into a permanently temporary one. This is just a miracle of modern politics: a scenario of a government that is always telling the people that it is about to leave, yet never actually leaving.

The recent constitutional amendments that give the president powers to care-take, and the care-taking presidential decrees that dissolved the government, were as clear as muddy water from the edge of the Nile. Nobody knows how many caretaker ministers were granted by the amendment to lead the country to elections, because apparently nobody knows when those elections will happen either. The plan seems to be: keep everyone guessing until guessing becomes the official public policy.

Now rumors are flowing like the sips of tea on Hai Thoura streets. The National Election Commission's elections preparation may be disbanded in November 2026 to make way for a new transitional government. The current government is secretly supporting this idea, but publicly acting shocked and offended when hearing the public discuss it. It wants the international community to pressure it, so it can later say, "We didn't want this, but our partners forced us. What could we do?" It is political theater at its finest, starring a government that wants to be saved from itself.

Meanwhile, our investigation has found out that the UN Security Council is being pushed by the current government's regional allies to pressure for another political settlement rather than elections. The process is likely yielding the intended purpose, as the UN Security Council has warned South Sudan through IGAD to release detained SPLM-IO leaders and form a unity government by January 2027. As this is the ongoing process that will happen, The Watchdog Press sees the upcoming political settlement as a masterpiece of confusion and illegitimacy that has never existed before; it is a constitutional crisis that never existed before. A government formed under pressure, with no clear rules, no real elections, and everyone pretending to be partners while sharpening their knives behind the curtains.

The truth is simple: South Sudan's leaders have turned transition into a permanent business. Elections are always coming, but never arriving. Unity governments are formed, dissolved, and recycled like plastic bottles. The only thing that changes is the size of the cars and the number of bodyguards, and the rest are the same game of the last 15 years.

So what will January 2027 bring? Probably another agreement, another extension, another caretaker government, and another speech about peace. The people will clap, the diplomats will nod, and the cycle will continue. In South Sudan, even the transition has a transition. And the only thing more confusing than the politics is the fact that everyone still pretends to be surprised. Till then!

25th September 2026

To: H.E. Gen. Salva Kiir Mayardit
President of the Republic of South Sudan

RE: HUMBLE APPEAL FOR CONSIDERATION OF THE 10 STATE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLIES ON MOBILITY SUPPORT AND MEDICINAL ALLOWANCES AND THREE ADMINISTRATIVE AREAS 

Your Excellency,

1. APPRECIATION
Allow me, on behalf of the Former Members of the 10 State Legislative Assemblies of the Republic of South Sudan, to convey our heartfelt appreciation to your leadership for maintaining peace and steering the nation through the Revitalized Transitional Period from 2020 since the formation to the dissolution day, 22nd September 2026. We remain committed and loyal to your leadership as President of the Republic South Sudan.

2. PURPOSE
Your Excellency, we have learned with appreciation that Members of the National Legislative Assembly (TNLA & Council of States) have been promised official vehicles to facilitate their work.

We humbly wish to bring to your attention that Members of the 10 State Legislative Assemblies across the country share the same constitutional mandate but have served from 17th November 2021 to 22nd December 2026 without mobility support and medical allowances.

3. PLIGHT OF THE 10 STATES AND THREE ADMINISTRATIVE AREAS ASSEMBLIES:
Your Excellency, Members of the 10 State Assemblies - from Northern Bahr El Ghazal, Western Bahr El Ghazal, Warrap, Lakes, Unity, Upper Nile, Jonglei, Central Equatoria, Eastern Equatoria and Western Equatoria and three administrative areas have served under very difficult conditions:
a) No regular salaries;
b) No medical cover and allowances;
c) No car loans or mobility facilitation;
d) Yet tasked to reach deep, insecure, and road-inaccessible constituencies.

Your Excellency, it is with deep sorrow that we inform you that the 10 State Legislative and three administrative Assemblies have lost many Honourable Members during our tenure from 2021 to 2026, not because of war, but due to lack of medical treatment and medical allowances.

Many colleagues died from treatable illnesses in Aweil, Juba, Kuajok, Wau, Bor, Malakal and other state capitals simply because there was no medical cover, no medical allowance, and no salary to afford referral abroad or even to Juba Teaching Hospital. We buried our fellow lawmakers while serving this nation, in silence and in poverty.

Your Excellency, provision of mobility and medical consideration is therefore not only a matter of welfare, but a matter of life and dignity for those who served this country at state level under your leadership.

It is disheartening that National Legislators are considered for cars while State Legislators who are directly with the people in the villages are left without any means of movement.

4. HUMBLE PRAYER
Your Excellency, we humbly appeal to your fatherly consideration to extend the mobility facilitation program to include Former Members of the 10 State Legislative Assemblies and three administrative areas.

We are not asking for luxury, Your Excellency, but for a tool to continue mobilizing our people for peace and preparing for elections as we return to our respective Constituencies, including my own Constituency No: 18  in NBGS-A. We trust in your wisdom and generosity.

Long live the President! 
Long live South Sudan!
Long live NBGS-Aweil!

Hon. Majook Madut Gar Malong 
Former Member of Parliament 
NBGS-A State Legislative Assembly
On Behalf of Former Members of the 10 States Legislative Assemblies and three administrative areas.

The Deng Tong Kenjok White-collar Rebellion: Why his arrogant and reckless Labour Policy will become a National Security Threat and a recipe for SPLM Election Failure

By Senior Staff Writer

South Sudan may be witnessing an unusual form of political rebellion, not through guns, uniforms or parliamentary forces, but through the workplace.
At the centre of the growing controversy is Deng Tong Kenjok, Undersecretary in the national Ministry of Labour, and his administration of the implementation of the National Social Insurance Fund (NSIF) Act, 2023.

The question is no longer simply whether South Sudan needs a social insurance system. It is whether the system is being introduced in a manner that protects workers, preserves confidence in government institutions and avoids destabilising the very economy upon which the state depends.
Public reporting indicates that Circular No. 5/2026 requires employers including private companies, NGOs, diplomatic missions and other organizations employing 5.09 million people (according to the world bank estimate) South Sudanese to register workers and remit social-insurance contributions directly to NSIF. Registration is scheduled to begin on 1 October 2026.

That is a major national policy decision at a time the country is entering elections  and where multiple rebel groups have surrounded Juba and other areas of the country, and at a time the country’s economy has collapsed and only in survival mode with the help of the very oil companies and humanitarian workers Deng Tong Kenjok are now pushing to the brink of labour crisis and possible rebellion or not vote for SPLM in the upcoming elections. Negative labour policies globally and historically have sparked rebellions or citizens anger with the ruling party.

But the controversy has moved beyond ordinary administrative disagreement. Workers' unions representing employees in the oil sector, NGOs and other private-sector organizations have challenged the implementation in courts, citing concerns over governance, transparency, legal authority, stakeholder consultation and the operational readiness of the Fund. The employees are threatening strikes or demonstrations  which if they occur, may be infiltrated by rebel groups and overthrow the regime. The employees are also threatening not to vote for SPLM if their money is forcefully taken.

This is where Deng Tong Kenjok's role deserves serious scrutiny.

If the reported position coming from the Labour Ministry is that employees and employers must remit contributions regardless of unresolved questions surrounding systems, safeguards and institutional readiness, then the Ministry is taking a remarkably rigid approach to a policy involving millions of workers.

A government can compel compliance but not acceptance. But compulsion without confidence is a dangerous administrative strategy that could spark labour and subsequently political crisis. 
The private sector is not an enemy of the state. Neither are NGOs, diplomatic missions, humanitarian organizations or oil companies. They are major components of South Sudan's economic and institutional ecosystem.

If confidence collapses among these constituencies, the consequences could extend far beyond payroll deductions.

A labour dispute in an ordinary commercial sector is one thing.

A labour dispute simultaneously involving oil workers, humanitarian organizations, NGOs, diplomatic missions, private companies and national employees is something entirely and seriously different.

Oil production is strategically important to South Sudan's economy. Oil workers ensure the oil is flowing to the international market and money flows back to the country to finance state operations including the Office of President Kiir, the National Security Service,the SSPDF, Police, Prison and other institutions. The NGOs, International Organisations and firms provide essential services to millions of vulnerable people in the form of operational health facilities, food distribution, nutritional supplies, water supplies , electricity and other critical services. Private companies sustain employment and commerce. Diplomatic missions and international organizations form part of the country's external economic, diplomatic and development architecture.

A prolonged labour confrontation affecting these sectors could therefore create an economic and governance crisis far larger than the original NSIF dispute.

That is why the conduct and public messaging of senior Labour Ministry officials deserve scrutiny.
Is this administrative determination, a reckless escalation or an incitement to rebel and not vote for the SPLM?

There is an important distinction between enforcing a law and insisting on implementation without adequately resolving legitimate institutional concerns. The Deng Tong Kenjok action is pure recklessness, institutional recklessness and dangerous strategy aimed at inciting the 5.09 millions to go on streets which will be infiltrated by the nearby SPLA-IO, NAS and other rebel groups, or overwhelmingly send President Kiir home.

Workers' representatives have not simply rejected social insurance. Their public position has been that they support the principle of social protection but object to the manner in which the NSIF framework is being implemented.
That distinction matters.

South Sudan needs social insurance.

South Sudan also needs an NSIF that workers trust.
Those two objectives are not contradictory.
Indeed, they are inseparable.

The government's own NSIF structures have been developing regulations, governance policies, communication strategies and engagement mechanisms, according to recent reporting. That suggests that the institutional architecture is still evolving.

So why rush the confrontation?

Why turn a potentially constructive social-protection reform into a confrontation between government and organized labour?

Why allow an administrative disagreement to reach the point where workers are before the courts and threatening demonstration and rebellion? 
And why risk creating an environment in which a technical question about social-insurance deductions becomes a broader question about confidence in government?

The language of rebellion

From April to date, after hearing of Elections this December, Deng Tong Kenjok with his errand boys who are well-known thieves in the public sector like Office of the President and quack lawyers unlicensed by the Bar Association have been telling Oil companies, NGOs and private sector companies to pay the NSIF deductions immediately whether there is a system, no staff, the South Sudan Pension Fund is a failure or success, etc or not, the employers MUST PAY whether they like it or not. Workers are wondering whether this is protection or robbery. And whether this is a careful labour directive or reckless one that harass workers into demonstration, strike and vote against SPLM, and diplomatic community to leave and further sanction South Sudan.

Some observers may therefore describe the current confrontation as a form of "white-collar rebellion" because dangerous labour policies implemented through sensitive workplaces can have consequences comparable to those produced by conventional political and military confrontation.
This posture and weaponization of Labour policies as tools for regime change should concern the President Kiir regime then it would concern workers.

Because once workers stop seeing the NSIF dispute as a technical administrative matter and genuine social protection and begin seeing it as a daylight robbery of their salaries, savings and institutional trust, the dispute can rapidly become political and militarized. History has it that good number of revolutions including South Sudan secession from Sudan, are sparked by negative labour policies such as sham contributory scheme, over taxation, discrimination in employment, etc.

And South Sudan has enough political fragility without manufacturing another crisis.
Deng Abbas should understand the power of the office he occupies.

The Undersecretary of Labour is not merely an administrator.

He sits at the intersection of government, employers, workers, trade unions, international organizations and the private sector.
That position demands consultation, restraint and confidence-building.

The Ministry itself says its mandate includes protecting employees and employers and encouraging collective bargaining.
The test, therefore, is not whether the Ministry can issue directives.

The test is whether it can implement them without destroying the confidence of the people and institutions expected to comply.
A social insurance system cannot succeed merely because workers and employers are ordered to contribute.
It succeeds when workers believe that their contributions are safe.
It succeeds when employers understand the rules.
It succeeds when the institution managing workers' money is trusted.
It succeeds when employers and employees are part of its governance.

And it succeeds when government listens before confrontation becomes litigation, demonstration and labour crisis, losing faith in the political establishment/leadership of the country, or a rebellion.

South Sudan does not need another avoidable crisis
The NSIF controversy should therefore be urgently de-escalated by firing Deng Tong Kenjok or Deng Abbas (Jena Aram) and all his errand boys in the NSIF including unlicensed lawyer Reech Ring, 8-months quack lawyer Akur Majeep (aka thief in the Office of the President), thief Kon Kelei, thief of donor money Elijah Manyok Jok and other clueless dudes in the NSIF.

The Deng Tong Kenjok White-collar Rebellion: Why his arrogant and reckless Labour Policy will become a National Security Threat and a recipe for SPLM Election Failure.

By Senior Staff Writer

South Sudan may be witnessing an unusual form of political rebellion, not through guns, uniforms or parliamentary forces, but through the workplace.
At the centre of the growing controversy is Deng Tong Kenjok, Undersecretary in the national Ministry of Labour, and his administration of the implementation of the National Social Insurance Fund (NSIF) Act, 2023.

The question is no longer simply whether South Sudan needs a social insurance system. It is whether the system is being introduced in a manner that protects workers, preserves confidence in government institutions and avoids destabilising the very economy upon which the state depends.
Public reporting indicates that Circular No. 5/2026 requires employers including private companies, NGOs, diplomatic missions and other organizations employing 5.09 million people (according to the world bank estimate) South Sudanese to register workers and remit social-insurance contributions directly to NSIF. Registration is scheduled to begin on 1 October 2026.

That is a major national policy decision at a time the country is entering elections  and where multiple rebel groups have surrounded Juba and other areas of the country, and at a time the country’s economy has collapsed and only in survival mode with the help of the very oil companies and humanitarian workers Deng Tong Kenjok are now pushing to the brink of labour crisis and possible rebellion or not vote for SPLM in the upcoming elections. Negative labour policies globally and historically have sparked rebellions or citizens anger with the ruling party.

But the controversy has moved beyond ordinary administrative disagreement. Workers' unions representing employees in the oil sector, NGOs and other private-sector organizations have challenged the implementation in courts, citing concerns over governance, transparency, legal authority, stakeholder consultation and the operational readiness of the Fund. The employees are threatening strikes or demonstrations  which if they occur, may be infiltrated by rebel groups and overthrow the regime. The employees are also threatening not to vote for SPLM if their money is forcefully taken.

This is where Deng Tong Kenjok's role deserves serious scrutiny.

If the reported position coming from the Labour Ministry is that employees and employers must remit contributions regardless of unresolved questions surrounding systems, safeguards and institutional readiness, then the Ministry is taking a remarkably rigid approach to a policy involving millions of workers.

A government can compel compliance but not acceptance. But compulsion without confidence is a dangerous administrative strategy that could spark labour and subsequently political crisis. 
The private sector is not an enemy of the state. Neither are NGOs, diplomatic missions, humanitarian organizations or oil companies. They are major components of South Sudan's economic and institutional ecosystem.

If confidence collapses among these constituencies, the consequences could extend far beyond payroll deductions.

A labour dispute in an ordinary commercial sector is one thing.

A labour dispute simultaneously involving oil workers, humanitarian organizations, NGOs, diplomatic missions, private companies and national employees is something entirely and seriously different.

Oil production is strategically important to South Sudan's economy. Oil workers ensure the oil is flowing to the international market and money flows back to the country to finance state operations including the Office of President Kiir, the National Security Service,the SSPDF, Police, Prison and other institutions. The NGOs, International Organisations and firms provide essential services to millions of vulnerable people in form of operational health facilities, food distribution, nutritional supplies, water supplies , electricity and other critical services. Private companies sustain employment and commerce. Diplomatic missions and international organizations form part of the country's external economic, diplomatic and development architecture.

A prolonged labour confrontation affecting these sectors could therefore create an economic and governance crisis far larger than the original NSIF dispute.

That is why the conduct and public messaging of senior Labour Ministry officials deserve scrutiny.
Is this administrative determination, a reckless escalation or an incitement to rebel and not vote for the SPLM?

There is an important distinction between enforcing a law and insisting on implementation without adequately resolving legitimate institutional concerns. The Deng Tong Kenjok action is pure recklessness, institutional recklessness and dangerous strategy aimed at inciting the 5.09 millions to go on streets which will be infiltrated by the nearby

JUBA, September 22, 2026 — South Sudan's transitional government has been dissolved, President Salva Kiir Mayardit announced today, paving the way for long-awaited general elections on December 22, 2026.

The declaration came during an expanded presidency meeting attended by vice presidents, political party leaders, presidential advisors, and senior ministers. A formal resolution is expected later today in line with the legal framework governing the electoral process.

"I have today dissolved the transitional government of national unity," Kiir said, calling the move "a decisive step toward returning power to the people."

The announcement marks a critical milestone in the 2018 revitalized peace agreement, which had repeatedly extended the transitional period. Opposition leaders present at the meeting reportedly welcomed the dissolution but urged the government to guarantee a free and fair vote.

The United Nations and regional bodies have yet to issue formal statements. Political analysts warn that logistical and security challenges could still threaten the December timeline, despite today's breakthrough.

More details are expected in a presidential decree to be issued later today.

This is a developing story. Updates to follow.

text:
The "Homeboy" Handshake: How to Break Protocol and Keep Your Job in South Sudan

Ladies and gentlemen, today, we have witnessed the absolute peak of "Muony Awan" privilege in J-1. Forget diplomatic protocols; forget the sacred rulebook of official ceremonies that used to be done with safari suits and big-size necktie. In this government, if you are from the right village, you can practically show up to a presidential swearing-in ceremony in your pajamas, sipping a cup of tea, and still keep your job. What a historical indirect disrespect to President Kiir. Actually General John Manut Wol was 100% right describing Gabriel Bol as a source of damage to Kiir Mayardit.

Let's talk about Gabriel Bol Deng, the newly appointed Elections Commission Chairman. This man didn't just attend a solemn state function; he treated it like a casual weekend visit to his old friend at the bar for drinks, look at the photo! The President is in a sharp suit, tie, and signature hat, looking every bit the Head of State. And Brother Gabriel? He showed up in a casual Jalabiya, looking like he just rolled out of bed to go buy groceries.

But the outfit is only half the comedy, it is just like a Nigerian movie outfit. The real slap in the face is the handshake. In many African cultures, placing your left hand on someone's back during a handshake is a massive, unmistakable sign of deep disrespect and the funniest mockery of a peer among themselves. I mean, it is a gesture reserved for your peer or your child. Yet, here is our big brother Gabriel, casually dropping his left hand on the President's right-back arm like they are two old men arguing over the price of sorghum at Custom Market.

Why? Because he is Muony Awan. He is the homeboy. He doesn't care about the official ceremony, and apparently, he doesn't care about the President's status. He is basically saying, "Hey! Salva, my guy!, just relax, it's just us. Let's go and have some drinks in Hong-Kong or Amanjam."

Now, let's apply some logic and remember the brutal double standards of this government. Flashback to May 6, 2016. President Salva Kiir literally forced the former Minister of Water and Irrigation, Hon. Mabior Garang de Mabior, to walk out of a Council of Ministers meeting just because he didn't like his dressing style. Though he was in Safari Suit, Mabior was just sent out because he had dressed in a bow-tie rather than a neck-tie. If you are from somewhere, one wrong shirt, and you are out the door!

But today? Today, the rules have changed, just overnight. What used to be a fireable offense is now just normal business if you belong to the right tribe. If Gabriel Bol Deng was from any other communities, he would have been thrown out of the hall, his appointment revoked, and his Jalabiya torn into pieces by security before he could even blink.

But because he is a homeboy, he gets a free pass. It is not arrogance; it is simply the ultimate VIP pass of tribal nepotism. The rest of South Sudan has to wear a suit and necktie, but for the Muony Awan? They just show up in their night dress, shake hands like a boss, and dare the system to do anything about it. Truly, it is good to be the homeboy!

Breaking News: South Sudan's Parliament Passes Contested Electoral Reforms Ahead of Scheduled Polls

Juba, South Sudan — In a landmark legislative move, the National Legislature has passed the National Elections Act, 2012 (Amendment) Bill, 2026, in its entirety, including all provisions and amendments.

The newly passed bill permits the incumbent President to remain in office with full constitutional powers throughout the election period. Additionally, it provides for the removal of the First Vice President and other Vice Presidents three months before the elections are held.

The development marks a significant shift in the country's electoral framework ahead of the scheduled polls. The bill now awaits the President's assent to become law. Once signed, the amendments will formally take effect, reshaping the roles of the executive during the transitional election period.

Observers say the changes could have far-reaching implications for the political landscape and the conduct of the upcoming elections. The presidency has not yet indicated when the bill will be signed. However, the Revitalized Agreement on the Resolution of the Conflict in South Sudan is set to expire on 22 December 2026. With this amendment, the government is expected to be dissolved sooner rather than later if it is signed into law by the President.

text:
The Politics of Proximity to Power

Brigadier General Lual Akeen’s political lifestyle, as perceived by many observers, reflects a troubling politics of proximity to power: friendship with those who hold office, silence when their power disappears, and renewed closeness whenever another centre of authority emerges.

Such politics reduces public relationships to appointments, influence and access. A person who values power more than principle will naturally disappear when the source of power disappears—like a creature retreating from smoke when its hiding place is disturbed.

There is also a broader concern about a political culture in which personal connections, inducements and loyalty to individuals are treated as substitutes for education, merit, institutional credentials and integrity. If allegations of bribery, opportunistic alliances or betrayal are made, they should be tested against evidence rather than political gossip.

South Sudan does not need politics built around proximity to the powerful. It needs institutions stronger than individuals, merit stronger than money, loyalty to principles stronger than loyalty to appointments, and public service stronger than personal advancement.

Power is temporary. Positions expire. Political fortunes change. What remains is character, and history eventually records it.

Authored by Monydeng Mijok Chol

President Salva Kiir Mayardit and His Brother-in-law Gregory Vasilis Have Been Using General Akech Tong Aleu as a Tool to Eliminate Tonj Politicians

By Ngor Ater Jel, Pharmaceutical Student, University of Juba

Information emerging from open sources, including statements associated with Morris Mabior Awikjok, described as a close associate of General Akech Tong Aleu, is bringing to the surface a political pattern that has for years been denied by General Akech Tong and those who defend his political activities.

The political games that have long been conducted behind closed doors are increasingly becoming visible. The central concern is the continued political pressure being directed against prominent politicians from Tonj and the apparent effort to weaken their influence within the government.

At present, Director General Akech Tong is working persistently to secure the removal of Minister Aleu Ayieny Aleu from the government as soon as possible. Akech Tong has stated that he is undertaking this mission on behalf of the President of the Republic.

Over the years, a number of prominent Tonj political figures have faced political setbacks, removals, or declining influence. The names associated with this broader pattern include Andrew Kuac Mayiik, Lewis Anei Madut Kuendit, the late Anthony Bol Madut, Lino Makan Akol, Mayiik Ayii Deng, Nhial Deng Nhial, Akol Koor Kuc, Christo Thon Magoordit, Yel Mayar Mareng, Achuil Akoch Magar, Dr. Riak Gok Majok, and now Minister Aleu Ayieny Aleu.

The issue therefore goes beyond one minister or one government position. It concerns whether Tonj politicians are being systematically weakened one after another, and whether political influence is being concentrated in the hands of a small group of individuals who claim to act in the interests of the Presidency.

The current campaign against Minister Aleu Ayieny Aleu has become particularly significant because it is connected to the Ministerial High-Level Committee on Economic Reforms. The committee was established to address some of the country's most serious economic challenges. Attempts to remove or politically discredit a minister involved in such a process therefore deserve public scrutiny, particularly when the justification for such action appears insufficient to many observers.

The people of Tonj should now pay close attention to the political developments taking place around their representatives. They should ask fundamental questions: Why have several influential Tonj politicians experienced political marginalization or removal? Why does the same political pattern continue to emerge? Who benefits from the weakening of Tonj's political representation? And why is General Akech Tong repeatedly associated with efforts that affect the political careers of fellow Tonj leaders?

It is also important to examine and strike powerfully the relationship between General Akech Tong, Gregory Vasilis, and President Salva Kiir Mayardit within this political context. The concern being raised is that these relationships have created a political network capable of influencing the appointment, removal, and survival of Tonj politicians within the government.

If this political pattern continues unchecked, the consequences will extend beyond individual politicians. It could weaken Tonj's collective political voice, reduce its ability to defend legitimate interests within the national government, and create divisions among leaders and communities that should instead be working together.

Tonj Community should therefore reject political divisions, personality-driven politics, and the practice of turning one Tonj leader against another for the benefit of individuals. Political disagreements are normal in a democratic society, but the removal or political destruction of leaders should never become a mechanism for weakening an entire community's representation.

The people of Tonj people should in one voice demonstrates a demand that they deserve transparency, accountability, and political fairness. Any decision concerning the future of Minister Aleu Ayieny Aleu should be based on clear evidence, established procedures, and the national interest—not on personal political rivalries or instructions attributed to powerful individuals.

The question before Tonj is no longer simply whether one politician will remain in government. The larger question is whether Tonj will continue losing one political voice after another while remaining silent.

Tonj must pay attention, remain united, and demand answers. No individual politician should be treated as disposable, and no community should be politically weakened through internal manipulation.

The time has come for Tonj leaders and citizens to look beyond individual political positions and examine the broader political pattern affecting their community.

NO NEGOTIATIONS OR AGREED DEAL TO RELEASE DR. RIEK MACHAR AND APPOINT HIS WIFE ANGELINA AS VICE PRESIDENT

This statement serves to clarify the situation surrounding claims of a political arrangement to secure the release of Dr. Riek Machar, relocate him to another country for retirement, and pave the way for Hon. Angelina Teny to become the only Vice President of the Republic of South Sudan following the next elections.

According to our reliable sources in Juba, this narrative has been deliberately manufactured by groups associated with Nathaniel Oyet and Stephen Par Kuol to create mistrust between Hon. Angelina Teny and the supporters of Dr. Riek Machar.

The objective is to portray Hon. Angelina Teny as someone prepared to advance her political position at the expense of her husband. That narrative is false. Hon. Angelina Teny would not accept a political arrangement that compromises Dr. Riek Machar’s political rights, position, or legitimate participation in the affairs of South Sudan.

South Sudanese politics has experienced serious divisions and painful betrayals, but individual actions should never be generalized to entire communities. Political narratives must be assessed on facts rather than manufactured accusations designed to create suspicion and division.

The position is clear: there is no negotiated arrangement or agreed deal to release Dr. Riek Machar, relocate him abroad for retirement, and replace him with Hon. Angelina Teny as Vice President of the Republic of South Sudan.

The supporters of Dr. Riek Machar should remain united, calm, and vigilant against misinformation intended to divide them.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

text:
If Elections Fail, What Happens Next? South Sudan Needs a Clear Constitutional Answer

By Peace Advocate Michael Manyiel Chol

As South Sudan approaches the scheduled general elections on 22 December 2026, one important question deserves serious national attention: What happens if the elections can not take place as planned? 

This is not a question intended to discourage elections. On the contrary, it is a call for constitutional clarity, political dialogue, and preparedness. The people of South Sudan deserve to know what legal framework will govern the country if the electoral timetable is not met.

The concern is particularly important because the transitional period has already been extended several times, and the current transition is expected to run until February 2027. UNMISS has also publicly expressed concern about whether the necessary political, security, and institutional conditions for credible, peaceful, and inclusive elections can be established in time. 

The central question is, therefore, simple:

If the elections fail to take place in December 2026, what happens to the Transitional Government of National Unity?

Does the existing transitional government continue? Is there another constitutional or political mechanism for extending the transition? Does the president continue exercising the presidency while the positions of the vice presidents and other transitional institutions are affected? Or must the political parties negotiate and establish another arrangement?

These questions should not be answered through political assumptions. They should be answered through the Constitution, the Revitalized Peace Agreement, subsequent constitutional amendments, and any legally adopted extension arrangements.

The original Transitional Constitution provides that the president is the head of state and government, while the vice president is part of the national executive. It also provides rules concerning vacancies in the presidency and the appointment of vice presidents. However, the current transitional arrangement was created and modified through the peace agreement and subsequent extensions, including the special power-sharing structure involving the First Vice President and four Vice Presidents. 

Therefore, we should not simply assume that the failure of an election automatically means the dissolved transitional government returns, nor should we assume that the president automatically receives unlimited authority to appoint a new government. The legal answer must come from the applicable constitutional and peace-agreement provisions in force at that time.

As a peace advocate, I believe this matter should be clarified before election day, not after a constitutional crisis emerges.

The presidency, political parties, National Legislative Assembly, Judiciary, civil society, youths, and the guarantors of the peace agreement should openly discuss the constitutional consequences of any electoral delay.

South Sudan has already experienced repeated extensions of its transitional period. We can not afford another situation where the country reaches a constitutional deadline without a clear and mutually accepted roadmap.

The question is not whether we want elections. We must prepare for elections. The question is whether we have prepared a lawful and peaceful contingency if the elections can not take place.

The Greater Pibor Administrative Area is currently facing concerns regarding governance and representation.

Hon. Gola Boyoi, the current Chief Administrator, is proposing the appointment of Mr. Lothila Gain, a close associate from his village and age-set, Lanngo, as the incoming Caretaker Chief Administrator of GPAA.

This proposal comes at a time when various GPAA communities have expressed dissatisfaction with the current administration, citing favoritism, division, and governance based on village and age-set affiliations rather than merit and community interest. Critics state that since his appointment, key positions and advisory roles have disproportionately been allocated to individuals from the National Congress Party age-set, Langgo, predominantly from the Chief Administrator’s village.

The administration is also facing scrutiny from Murle community members who state that current policies do not place the community at the center of decision-making and have contributed to divisions among communities and youth.

Responsibilities

We call on the Government of South Sudan and the relevant national authorities to ensure that any caretaker appointment in the Greater Pibor Administrative Area follows a transparent, lawful, inclusive, and accountable process.

The leadership of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area has a responsibility to uphold fairness, avoid favoritism, and ensure that governance serves all communities rather than particular villages or age-sets.

Demands

We therefore demand:

1. A transparent and inclusive process for the appointment of any Caretaker Chief Administrator.

2. Meaningful consultation with the diverse communities of GPAA before any appointment is finalized.

3. Clear and publicly communicated selection criteria based on competence, integrity, experience, and community interest.

4. An end to appointments based on personal relationships, village affiliation, or age-set connections.

5. Equal consideration and representation of the diverse communities of GPAA in governance and advisory positions.

6. Accountability and openness throughout the appointment process to prevent further divisions and restore public confidence.

The people of the Greater Pibor Administrative Area deserve leadership that promotes unity, fairness, inclusion, and the common interest of all communities.

By Watchdog Press's Coordinator in Pibor Administrative Area

Breaking News: President Kiir May Skip UN Trip, H.E. Adut Kiir Tipped to Represent Him - Said DG Akech Tong Aleu 

According to reliable sources in Juba, President Salva Kiir Mayardit is likely to pull back from his planned trip to the United States for the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

This disclosure was made by NSS Director General Akech Tong Aleu. Speaking to sources close to the matter, DG Akech, who heads the Internal Security Bureau (ISB), hinted that the President may instead send his daughter, Adut Kiir, to represent him at the World's high-level gathering in New York.

DG Akech Tong further explained that the reason behind the possible change of plan is linked to the size of the delegation supposedly accompanying the President.

According to him and sources he spoke to them, President Kiir had demanded a fifty-member delegation to accompany him to New York. This demand, however, was reportedly not granted, with the approved number said to be much less than fifty. As a condition for travelling, DG Akech said the President is said to be insisting on his full list, and if it is not accepted, he would rather not go. DG Akech directly blamed Hon. Tut Gatluak Manime and Hon. Adut Salva Kiir, including what he described as helpless Ministers of Presidential Affairs and of Foreign Affairs, for their failures to use alternative means in advance by convincing President Museveni and PM Abyei Ahmed, who would have softened the way for a huge delegation to New York. 

If this holds, in accordance with how things are locally happening in Juba, it would not be the first time a head of State unexpectedly sends a close family member or a Senior Envoy to the UN General Assembly, but it would certainly raise questions.

The UN General Assembly is the biggest diplomatic stage in the world. It is where presidents meet bilateral partners, where investors are courted, and where a country's position on global issues is made clear. For South Sudan, which is facing economic pressure, political transition questions, and a dire humanitarian situation, representation matters.

Sending H. E. Adut Kiir - who has increasingly been seen in diplomatic engagements is not a bad decision but would be seen by some people and organizations as a sign of trust and continuity. And of course, by others, it would be seen as a missed opportunity for direct Presidential engagement at a time when direct engagement is most needed to help South Sudan's top leadership get favor from there.

For now, the public is waiting to see what will actually happen. As DG Akech himself put it, people are waiting to see what his hint will look like in reality very soon.

Will President Kiir eventually board the plane with a smaller delegation? Will Adut Kiir indeed step onto the UN podium? Or will there be a last-minute compromise on the fifty-member demand?

Until an official statement comes from the Office of the President or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, this remains information attributed to the General of the ISB - not an official position from the presidency

But in Juba, where such information spreads fast, the debate has already started.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future
