Part One: How Brigadier General Akot Abiem Akeen, the Brother of Slay Queen – Becky Akuindik Abiem Shamefully Betrayed People

In 2013–2014, during the Aguok Kuei community conference that was held in Gogrial Town, Akot Abiem was there as the MC who facilitated the conference. At that time, he was also a strong supporter of Makiir Gai Thiep.

However, things did not go in their favor because some Spear Masters from Aguok Chiek rejected Makiir Gai as community leader. Instead, they chose the late Honorable Lual from the Wuny section. This led to disagreement because the people were from different sides, and the conference was canceled. It was agreed to hold it another year, but no leader was chosen before it was called off.

Then, in 2015, when Akot Abiem was serving as a minister in Gogrial State during the period of the 32 states, he came up with another plan to get money. In the evening, he contacted Makiir Gai and told him, “If you give me ten million South Sudanese pounds, I will recommend you as Aguok Kuei community leader because I am still a minister.”

They came to an agreement. But Makiir asked him, “What about the Spear Masters who rejected me last time, and the chiefs?”

Akot then came up with a plan: “If you buy a car for that one Spear Master and give more cash to the other Spear Masters and chiefs, then you will be recommended as community leader.” He also assured Makiir that more money would be given to the commissioner.

After all those conditions were fulfilled according to Akot Abiem’s instructions, two days later, in the evening, Makiir was announced as the Aguok Kuei community leader on state radio. This was based on Akot Abiem’s plan. Akot even went as far as forging the signatures of some chiefs without their knowledge. The chiefs were surprised when they heard it on the radio.

In December 2022, there was supposed to be a conference held. However, Akot opposed the conference because Makiir Gai had given him $10,000. Akot Abiem mobilized some community youths in Juba and Aguok. He also mobilized family members, including Simon Mou Abiem, William Akot Mou, Valentino Aken Mou, Morris Mou Abiem, Angelo Mathiek Ring, Agany Agany, Thel Bak, and other people whom I did not mention.

Because of their plan, the conference did not take place that year.

Later, in 2024, Akot moved to another business tycoon, Bibi Ali, because his former boss, Makiir Gai, had become broke. Akot then associated himself with Ali and designed another project to get money. He told Bibi Ali that there was a need to fund a proposed conference in Gogrial Town and that Ali would be named as a community leader. Ali accepted it because he is a good man, even though he would not actually become a community leader. Funds were mobilized, and the conference was fully funded.

However, when people reached Gogrial, Akot Abiem contacted Bibi at night and asked him for five thousand dollars. Mr. Ali told him, “There’s no money in my hand right now, but I can help you when we go back to Juba.”

After hearing that, Brigadier General Akot Abiem immediately betrayed Bibi. He then associated himself with Aweng Abior Deng. He proposed to Aweng that he should become a community leader. They promised each other that if Aweng Abior got the chance to become community leader, Aweng should recommend Akot Abiem as Governor of Warrap State.

Apparently, Aweng Abior recommended him through the Office of the First Lady. But when the letter reached the President, it was turned down because Akot Abiem has bad records that are known by the President.

Note: Part Two will be about how he allegedly betrayed family members, including Morris Mou Abiem, Angelo Mathiek Ring, Simon Mou Abiem, Aken Mou, William Akot Mou, Aken Aherdit, Sultan Ngor Mou Mou, and Agem Akotdit.

By Senior Citizen of Warrap State from Gogrial Community, the Republic of South Sudan

The Cry of Compassion and Patriotism: A Prominent Elder Eng. Valentino Malueth Akech Speaks on the Endless Twic Mayardit–Ngok Dinka Conflict

The painful and seemingly endless conflict between the Twic Mayardit and Ngok Dinka communities continues to raise serious questions about the loss of lives, the unresolved border question, and the urgent need for reason, compassion, and patriotism.

In a powerful statement reflecting both concern and historical experience, prominent elder and engineer Valentino Malueth Akech, a member of the Abyei Demarcation Team, offers his perspective on the technical and legal complexities surrounding the border between Twic Mayardit and Abyei.

“Twic and Ngok Dinka are allowed to kill themselves for no logical reason. The Abyei border, as delimited by the International Court of Arbitration in The Hague on the ninth of July 2009, was only three lines: the northern line, eastern line, and western line.

As the Border Technical Team that was tasked with the demarcation of the given lines, we did not have the mandate to do anything on the southern line that is separating South Sudan from Northern Sudan.

Therefore, the line separating Twic Mayardit from Abyei depends on the 1956 border, which has not been determined by the two countries. It is just an imaginary line that the two countries have not yet agreed on its process. So, it was wrong for Abyei to determine the border between Abyei and Twic before the 1956 border demarcation.

Doing that process will only be possible after the delimitation of the 1956 border between North and South and should be done by the Border Commission. Period.”

— Eng. Valentino Akech
Member, Abyei Demarcation Team

His statement is a powerful reminder that the loss of innocent lives over an unresolved boundary cannot be allowed to become a permanent reality. Whatever the historical, political, or administrative disagreements may be, the people of Twic Mayardit and Ngok Dinka deserve peace, justice, and a responsible process for resolving their differences.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

Juba, South Sudan – Senior Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM) figure Daniel Awet Akot has publicly endorsed recent statements by Vice President Rebecca Nyandeng Mabior, the widow of the party's founder Dr. John Garang de Mabior.

Awet, a veteran liberation hero and the SPLM 3rd Deputy Chairperson, affirmed that Nyandeng’s remarks were appropriate and necessary. "What Mama Rebecca said was in order," he stated. "We are the senior living members of the SPLM, and if we remain silent, who will speak on behalf of the people we liberated?" 

His comments come amid heightened political tensions, as the nation approaches elections scheduled for December 2026. Nyandeng recently used a public funeral service to launch a sharp critique of President Salva Kiir's administration, questioning who is advising the president and complaining about being denied access to him.

Awet’s support underscores the growing public discourse among the SPLM's founding generation regarding the country's leadership and direction. Both Nyandeng and Awet are part of the party's old guard, with Awet having served in various senior roles including Governor of Lakes State and Minister of Interior.

His defense of Nyandeng highlights the internal debates within the ruling party regarding its legacy and future.

text:
A RESPONSE TO ALEK PHILLIP MALUIL: EDUCATION DOES NOT EXEMPT ANYONE FROM ETHICS, CULTURAL RESPONSIBILITY, OR ACCOUNTABILITY

Alek Phillip Maluil, though we are seeing the handwriting of your Agany, be assured that your statement may be several pages long, but length does not automatically make an argument convincing. Sometimes, a thousand pages of explanation cannot repair a single fundamental question of integrity—especially when the public is left questioning the conduct, judgment, and respect for the cultural values surrounding a deeply sensitive family matter.

You repeatedly wrote, “I am an educated and grown woman,” as though education itself settles every moral, cultural, and ethical question. It does not. Education should increase one's sense of responsibility, humility, respect, and understanding of consequences—not simply provide a stronger vocabulary for defending oneself.

You also wrote, “Marriage should be built on love, mutual choice, and free will.” That principle deserves respect. But if you are invoking freedom and personal choice, then the public has every right to ask: where is the ethical responsibility toward the families, elders, relatives, and cultural institutions that traditionally participate in marriage negotiations?

South Sudanese culture is not a decorative background that we invoke when convenient and discard when inconvenient. Marriage, particularly within Jieeng communities, involves families, elders, dignity, negotiations, responsibilities, and social relationships. Modern education may change how young people understand marriage, but it does not automatically erase every cultural obligation.

And this is where your statement becomes particularly troubling.

You described the July 2026 marriage negotiation as having been conducted with “the support and agreement of our two families.” Yet your entire statement is framed around an intensely personal narrative in which your individual choice becomes the central—and almost exclusive—moral authority.

There is nothing wrong with choosing the person you love. But there is something profoundly wrong when personal freedom is presented as though it eliminates the need for cultural sensitivity, family accountability, and ethical conduct.

You further wrote, “I chose Agany, and I will continue to choose him.” Fine. That is your right. But the public is equally entitled to examine how that choice was pursued, communicated, defended, and presented to society.

And here is the uncomfortable question:

Where is the ethic here?

Where is the humility?

Where is the respect for the people whose families, emotions, dignity, and cultural relationships have become part of this controversy?

Where is the responsibility to de-escalate rather than turn a private family dispute into a nationwide social-media spectacle?

You cannot simultaneously demand that everyone respect your private choice while publishing an extensive public statement that invites millions of people to judge the character and conduct of members of your extended family.

That is not necessarily a defence of tradition. It may simply be another form of escalation.

And to Alek and Agany: whatever one thousand pages, ten thousand pages, or even millions of pages of clarifications, statements, interviews, books, or social-media explanations you may produce—none of them will automatically restore public confidence once reputation and trust have been seriously damaged.

Reputation is not repaired by volume.

It is repaired by conduct, accountability, restraint, honesty, time, and ethical behaviour.

You can write another statement tomorrow. You can write another one next week. You can publish a book next year. But if the underlying questions remain unanswered, the additional words will only make the controversy louder.

And perhaps the most revealing part of the entire statement is that you repeatedly invoke being “educated” while appearing to underestimate the importance of cultural intelligence.

A university degree can teach you how to read books.

It cannot automatically teach you how to navigate family dignity.

It cannot automatically teach you how to respect elders.

It cannot automatically teach you how to resolve sensitive cultural disputes.

And it certainly cannot make every personal decision morally unquestionable.

Education without wisdom can become arrogance. Freedom without responsibility can become recklessness. Love without respect can become conflict.

So before lecturing South Sudanese parents, men, communities, and traditional institutions about what they should or should not do, perhaps there should first be an honest examination of your own responsibilities, your own conduct, and the consequences of publicly framing a deeply complicated family matter in such absolute terms.

You ended by saying, “Let love, consent, and free choice guide marriage.”

Yes—let them.

But let respect, truth, responsibility, cultural understanding, humility, and ethical conduct guide it too.

Because consent is important.

Love is important.

Freedom is important.

But integrity is equally important.

And no amount of sophisticated English, emotional declarations, political accusations, or lengthy public explanations can substitute for it.

At some point, the public will stop listening to the explanations and start judging the conduct.

That is where the real test begins.

And yes, Alek—after all these explanations, the question remains painfully simple:

Where is the ethic here?

Or have we reached a point where being educated means believing that everyone else must surrender their cultural values, family dignity, and moral questions simply because you have declared your personal choice?

That is a debate worth having. And to be continued by Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

Statement on Reports of Rapid Support Forces (RSF) Armed Personnel in South Sudan and the Protection of National Sovereignty

Date: 25 August 2026
Issued by: Concerned South Sudanese

We, the undersigned citizens of the Republic of South Sudan, express our deep concern over recent reports and public anxiety regarding the alleged presence of foreign armed personnel within our territory, specifically in areas near Juba, including Terekeka County. So far, it is believed that 3,500 RSF armed personnel are inside the country.

South Sudan was born from the sacrifice of millions who fought for self-determination. Our Constitution and the Revitalized Peace Agreement guarantee that sovereignty belongs to the people. Any deployment of foreign forces on our soil touches the very foundation of that sovereignty.

Our Concerns

1. National Security and Public Trust
Rumors of foreign fighters in the name of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) being used for internal political purposes have created fear and confusion among citizens. Whether true or not, the government has a duty to address these concerns immediately with facts, not silence.

2. Risk of Regional Entanglement
With the ongoing conflict in Sudan, South Sudan must not be drawn into another war. Recruiting South Sudanese to fight in foreign conflicts, or hosting foreign fighters to do so, violates our national interest and endangers our fragile peace.

3. The Right to Choose Our Leaders
With national elections planned for December 2026, citizens must be assured that the electoral process will be free from intimidation and that security institutions will protect voters, not target them.

Our Demands

We call upon the Government of the Republic of South Sudan to:

1. Issue a Public Clarification within 72 hours on the presence or absence of RSF armed personnel in South Sudan, including their mandate, numbers, and legal basis.

2. Allow Independent Verification by UNMISS, IGAD, the African Union, and independent national media to access areas of concern and report to the public.

3. Uphold the Law: No foreign deployment should occur without approval from the National Legislature, as required by the Transitional Constitution.

4. Protect Civic Space: Guarantee that citizens, journalists, and activists can raise questions about national security without fear of arrest, harassment, or threats.

5. Prioritize South Sudanese Lives: Commit publicly that no South Sudanese will be recruited to fight in foreign wars and that our army and security services will remain focused on protecting our own borders and people.

Our Message to Citizens

Fear thrives in silence. We urge all South Sudanese to remain calm, reject hate speech, and demand answers through peaceful and lawful means. Our country belongs to all of us—not to any individual, family, or faction. The liberation struggle was for a South Sudan where the people decide.

The December elections must be the moment we return political choice to the people. That can only happen if we protect our sovereignty today.

A Drunk Man's Tale: Why Nhial Bol Aken Should Blame His Bottle, Not the General General Mike Mike

A certain desperate political orphan called Nhial Bol Aken is blaming  General Mike Mike just for political score.
There is a dangerous new pastime in South Sudan: dragging the names of our uniformed heroes through the mud for cheap political points. The latest target is Tiger Division Chief of Operations Brigadier General Mike Mike, and the accuser, if we can call him that, is former MP Nhial Bol. Let us call this what it is: a pathetic, drunken fabrication from a washed-up politician desperate to remain relevant.

General Mike Mike’s office has already put the matter to rest with crystal clarity. The commander, Mike Mike, was not even in the country when the incident at Nhial’s residence occurred. He was abroad on official duty. Yet Nhial Bol, in his usual theatrical fashion, rushed to the court of public opinion to insinuate that the General Mike Mike had personally orchestrated a siege against his home. This is not a security concern; this is character assassination by a man who has contributed nothing to national stability except hot air and empty bottles.

So, here is the things, it is fighting of two young men over the girl that lead security forces to raid Nhial house. Agany and Ariik are fighting over a girl like it’s the final match of a reality show. Ariik elopes with her (with mom’s blessing), but dad, who’s Team Agany, swoops in, snatches her back, and drops her off at Nhial’s house like a package, Nhial is the uncle of Agany. Girl's Mom become furious and rather die to see Agany as her son-in-law, called the local forces in the sector called joint operation, to raid Nhial’s Nhial house and retrieve the girl. Meanwhile, Nhial at the time was so drunk that he see every soldiers giant as a tigers wearing "Gen. Mike Mike" name tags on their badge. We can attest that this man cannot survive without his bottle; he probably offers the troops a sip before realizing they’re not there for a party. So now you’ve got love, betrayal, parents fighting, and a drunk uncle hallucinating jungle animals, truly a blockbuster in the making! Where is fault of Gen. Mike Mike here?

Let us examine the facts, which Nhial conveniently omits. The deployment of security forces and police was a routine, responsible response to a family dispute. specifically, the forceful elopement of a young girl, which had ignited tensions and threatened to spiral into neighborhood violence. The forces were dispatched to protect lives, including those in Nhial’s vicinity, and were withdrawn the moment calm was restored. That is called professionalism. That is what a disciplined force does. It does not pick sides; it restores order.

But Nhial Bol, perhaps nursing a hangover from his latest binge, saw an opportunity. He twisted a community safety operation into a personal vendetta against him. Why? Because a sober man would recognize that the military has better things to do than harass a retired legislator with delusions of grandeur. Nhial wants to defame General Mike Mike because the General represents the very discipline and integrity that Nhial lacks. He cannot attack the General’s record, so he attacks his character with baseless innuendo.

This is not about Nhial Bol. This is about protecting the reputation of our security forces from malicious slander. General Mike Mike has served this nation with honor. He does not need to intimidate a former MP; he has real enemies to fight. Nhial, on the other hand, should look in the mirror and ask why no one takes him seriously anymore. The answer is simple: his words carry no weight, only the stench of cheap liquor and bitter resentment.

We stand with General Mike Mike. We reject Nhial Bol’s defamatory circus. And we demand that our officers be allowed to do their jobs without every family dispute being weaponized into a political scandal by a has-been looking for his fifteen minutes of fame.

Breaking: NSS Chief General Akech Tong Aleu Orders Arrest of Vice President Rebecca Nyandeng, Saying President Kiir Directed Him

In a dramatic escalation of political tensions in South Sudan, National Security Service (NSS) Director General Akec Tong Aleu has reportedly ordered the immediate arrest of Vice President Rebecca Nyandeng de Mabior and placed the entire family of the late Dr. John Garang under surveillance.

According to sources at Juba International Airport, Vice President Nyandeng was prevented from boarding her scheduled flight to Nairobi this morning. Security operatives blocked her departure and informed her that her travel documents had been revoked. The NSS chief has additionally directed that all passports belonging to the Garang family be confiscated.

This development follows the Vice President's recent public criticism of President Salva Kiir Mayardit and his administration. Nyandeng had openly condemned what she described as a failure in service delivery and a lack of coordination within the government, particularly targeting the inefficiency of the presidential office. Her remarks, made during the church prayers of Late Kosti Manibe, appeared to have triggered the security response.

The critical question now centers on the chain of command: Is General Akec acting on his own authority, or is he executing orders from higher up? The involvement of President Kiir remains unclear, as does the possible role of Senior Presidential Envoy Adut Salva Kiir, who has severally been mentioned in connection with the directive.

This move carries significant political weight, as Vice President Nyandeng is a prominent figure in South Sudan's political landscape and a widow of the country's founding father. Placing her family under surveillance and restricting their movement suggests a deliberate strategy to neutralize dissent within the highest levels of government.

The timing raises concerns about the stability of the revitalized peace agreement, which relies on power-sharing arrangements between rival factions. Any action against a vice president especially one from a rival political camp, risks unraveling the fragile peace.

There has been no official statement from the presidency, the NSS, or Vice President Nyandeng's office at the time of this report. It remains to be seen whether diplomatic interventions will de-escalate the standoff or whether the government will press forward with the arrest.

As South Sudan watches this crisis unfold, many are questioning whether this marks a return to authoritarian tactics that defined earlier periods of conflict. The international community is also likely to weigh in, as actions targeting a sitting vice president could undermine donor confidence and regional stability.

STOP THE GRAB: HANDS OFF AFRICAN RESOURCES CORPORATION 

By: A Concerned Citizen
Juba | 22nd August 2026

South Sudan is watching a dangerous movie we have seen before. And we must say it loudly now before the credits roll: Stop the grabbing of ARC properties.

This week, a letter dated 21st August 2026  from the Ministry of Justice’s Investigation and Prosecution Committee gave African Resources Corporation (ARC)72 hours to surrender a full list of all its vehicles and properties. The letter cites Criminal Case No. 710/2026 and laws on anti-money laundering and criminal procedure.

On the surface, it looks like “law.” But context matters.

The owner of ARC, Former Vice President Benjamin Bol Mel, is currently under house arrest. He has not been convicted of any crime. He has not had his day in court. Yet institutions of the state are already moving to inventory, and effectively take control of the assets of his private company.

That is not justice. That is confiscation before trial.

1. You Cannot Punish a Man Before the c9ourt does
House arrest is a restriction of movement, not a conviction. 
The presumption of innocence is in our Transitional Constitution. It is also in the same Penal Code Act of 2008 that the Committee quoted in its letter.

If the state suspects a crime, investigate. Prosecute. Prove it in court. 
But you do not get to raid a company, seize its asset register, and paralyze its operations while the owner is locked in his home and cannot defend himself.

That is not due process. That is political targeting wearing legal clothes.

2. ARC is Not Government Property
African Resources Corporation is a private company. It employs South Sudanese. It pays taxes. It runs projects. 
Whether you like Benjamin Bol Mel or not, the company has workers, creditors, partners, and contracts that have nothing to do with Case 710/2026.

When you freeze or “request” all assets of a company this way, you don’t just target one man. You target hundreds of families who depend on ARC for salaries. You target suppliers in Konyo Konyo. You target the credibility of private investment in South Sudan.

Who will bring money into this country if companies can be dismantled by committee letter the moment their owner falls out of favor?

3. The Timing Stinks
Let’s call it what it is. 
The moment a senior leader is placed under house arrest, the machinery moves to go after his business. We saw it before. We are seeing it again. 

Using the Anti-Money Laundering Act and Criminal Procedure Act to demand asset lists within 72 hours is legal on paper. But using it selectively, without a conviction, is abuse.
If there is real evidence of crime, take it to court. Get a court order for seizure. Let lawyers argue. Let a judge decide.

“Committees” should not become courts.

4. This Hurts President Kiir and the Country
Mr. Juma Chirilo and others say they “support President Kiir.” The best way to support him is to protect the rule of law around him.

When the state is seen grabbing private property without trial, the President gets the blame. Investors get scared. Citizens lose faith. And our enemies get talking points: “South Sudan is not safe for business.”

Is that what we want?

Our Demands

1.  Stop the asset grab immediately. No seizure, no takeover, no interference with ARC operations until there is a court conviction.
2.  Take it to court.If there is a case, prosecute Benjamin Bol Mel fairly and publicly. Let him defend himself.
3.  Protect ARC workers.The state must guarantee that employees will not lose jobs because of a political case.
4.  Respect the Constitution. Investigation yes. Persecution no.

Final Word

South Sudan has buried too many people. We have also buried too many companies, too many jobs, and too much trust because we confuse politics with justice.

Former VP Benjamin Bol Mel deserves his day in court — not a midnight inventory of his company while he is under house arrest.
ARC deserves to operate under the law — not be dismantled by administrative letters.

If we allow this today, tomorrow it will be your company. Your land. Your car.

Hands off ARC. Let the law take its course. And let the court, not a committee, decide guilt or innocence.

Presented by Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

To: Larson Angok Garang  
Re: Your “Last Polite Response”

Larson Angok, 

Thank you for writing back. You said this is your last polite response. We will match your tone: direct, no insults, and focused on the issues — because the public deserves that.

Let’s go point by point.

1. "I should not explain the circumstances of Hon. Monica’s relief because no one ever has".
That’s exactly the problem. 

“You’ve never asked before” is not a defense. “We’ve never been transparent before” is not a principle. 
South Sudan cannot keep using “this is how we’ve always done it” to justify secrecy. 

You ask: “Who did she replace?” Fair question. The answer should be on record too. Two wrongs don’t make a right. 
If we want a professional civil service, then every appointment and relief must have a reason and a process. Not WhatsApp rumors. Not silence. A gazette, a statement, a reason. 
That’s not a “new standard.” That’s the minimum standard in any country that wants to fight corruption.

2. Watchdog Press is not a real media outlet
You’re entitled to your opinion of us. 

But here’s the test of a media outlet: Do we publish information the public cares about? Do we give the people named a chance to respond? Yes, we did — we published your full statement. 
Do we do live football and polls? No. Al Jazeera doesn’t either. The New York Times doesn’t stream football. That doesn’t make them less of a media house. 

You say we are “90% negative and target SPLM.” If 90% of the scandals, unpaid salaries, and sackings are coming from one side of government, then 90% of the reporting will be about that side. That’s not rebellion. That’s math.

Criticism is not rebellion. Abuse is not the same as accountability. If you think a specific story is false, sue us for defamation and let the court decide. That’s how democracies handle it.

3. You can’t demand the Office of the President to confirm staff
With respect, yes we can. And we must. 

The Presidency is funded by public money. The people who work there, their roles, and how they got there are matters of public interest — not state secrets. 
“Some issues must remain confidential” cannot mean “the entire organization chart is classified.” 
If Akolda is not a staff member, say so. If she is, say what her role and qualifications are. Silence breeds the exact rumors you’re trying to kill.

4. You admitted a Private Secretary can’t fire an Advisor, so why claim he’s powerful?
We didn’t say he fired her. We reported an allegation that influence was used. There’s a difference. 

And yes, in any presidency in the world, the person who controls the President’s diary, phone calls, and visitors has enormous influence. That’s not an insult. That’s political science 101.

It doesn’t mean the Private Secretary is “above the Minister.” It means proximity equals access, and access equals power. Pretending otherwise insults the intelligence of South Sudanese.

5. You will be located" is not a threat
Larson, you’re a lawyer. You know how this sounds. 

“Locating” unnamed journalists and then “bringing them to book” is the definition of intimidation. If you have a legal case, file it. The courts don’t require you to document  someone on Facebook first. 
Threats, veiled or not, push us further from the rule of law and closer to the politics of fear. As an Activist and Lawyer, I expected you to defend due process, not warn of extra-legal “surprises like a horse.”

6. The disrespect was about sexual advances and intoxication claims
If those specific claims are false, then prove them false. 
But lumping criticism of staff conduct with “disrespect to the President” is dangerous. It means no one can ever question anyone around the President ever again. 
That’s not protecting the President. That’s isolating him. The best way to protect H.E. Kiir’s legacy is to ensure his office operates with integrity and transparency.

7. I called you rebels because you target SPLM
That’s lazy. 

Holding the ruling party accountable is the job of the press in a democracy. SPLM has been in power for 20+ years. Of course most stories will involve SPLM officials. 
Calling critics “rebels” is how we shut down debate and how we got into this cycle of impunity. Patriots criticize their government. That’s how you make it better.

So where does this leave us?

You say you won’t engage further. That’s your choice. 

But here is what would actually end this back-and-forth today:
1. A statement from the Office of the President on the advisory office changes. No secrets, just facts.

2. A defamation case in court if we published lies. We will show up and defend our reporting.

3. Stop threatening journalists. Argue with us, debate us, but don’t threaten us.

Larson, you are a Veteran Artiste, Activist, and Lawyer. People listen to you. Use that voice to push for transparency, not to tell citizens to “disregard” and “be quiet.”

We don’t hate Akol Santo. We don’t hate the President. We love this country enough to ask hard questions.

If that makes us rebels in your eyes, then so be it.
,  
Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

STATEMENT BY THE TONJ COMMUNITY LEADERSHIP

Subject: Response to Issues Raised by H.E. Governor Bol Wek Agoth Regarding Tonj Community Affairs

The Tonj Community Leadership has learned with utter shock of a letter authored by H.E. Agoth Bol Wek Agoth, Governor of Warrap State, addressed to the Director General of the Internal Security Bureau (NSS), Gen. Akec Tong Aleu. In the letter, the Governor directs the cancellation of the planned Tonj Community Leadership elections in Juba. These were scheduled to begin with the formal dissolution of the current executive body on Saturday, 22nd August 2026, followed by a general election on a date to be determined by the General Assembly.

The Tonj Community Leadership is deeply dismayed by the hostile tone of the letter, which reflects underlying prejudice and factional politics. Rather than acting as a unifier and peacemaker, the Governor has allowed himself to be drawn into divisive political dynamics in Tonj. This letter represents a clear abuse of executive authority that exacerbates division within Greater Tonj.

In his letter, the Governor cites three main grounds for his intervention:

1. That the call to convene the General Assembly was not initiated by the Tonj Community Leader and that the Preparatory Committee acted without authority.

2. That local community elections must be restricted due to preparations for the upcoming national elections in December 2026.

3. That during an August 12, 2026 meeting of the Peacebuilding and Reconciliation Forum (allegedly chaired by Hon. Andrew Kuac Mayol Gai), an unnamed group presented demands that were “politically motivated” and intended to obstruct reconciliation in Warrap State. The letter claims these demands included dissolving the Greater Tonj Peacebuilding Forum, releasing Gen. Akol Koor Kuc from house arrest, separating Tonj from Warrap State, and dissolving the current community leadership structure.

The Tonj Community Leadership hereby sets the record straight: these grounds are entirely false, misrepresent reality, and serve only to create unwarranted confusion.

1. Authorization of the Preparatory Committee

In June 2026, Ustaz Lewis Anei Madut Kuendit issued a public notice to the Tonj community in Juba declaring his intention to step down, citing the expiration of his constitutional mandate.

On 15th June 2026, he formally constituted a Preparatory Committee responsible for organizing the upcoming elections and fundraising. Article 2 of the committee's Terms of Reference explicitly mandates them to “convene the General Assembly meeting for leadership dissolution and conduct the election of the Tonj Community Leader in Juba.”

The committee acted fully within its defined mandate; alleging otherwise is disingenuous.

2. Community Governance vs. National Elections

The argument that community elections must be suspended due to the upcoming national general elections lacks any legal basis. It is contradictory to halt local democratic processes under the guise of preparing for national democracy.

Community leadership elections in Juba do not violate state or national electoral laws; rather, they foster healthy democratic participation. There is no legal restriction precluding community associations from holding internal elections.

3. Misrepresentation of the August 12 Meeting

The meeting held on 12th August 2026 at the Quality Hotel was neither organized by the Peacebuilding and Reconciliation Committee nor chaired by Hon. Andrew Kuac Mayol Gai. It was chaired by Ustaz Lewis Anei Madut Kuendit at the request of Gen. Akec Tong Aleu, following a consultative visit by Tonj elders on 11th August 2026.

The documented agenda of the meeting focused entirely on unifying various peace committees into a cohesive framework under the Tonj Peacebuilding and Reconciliation umbrella. Demands regarding the release of Gen. Akol Koor Kuc, the territorial separation of Tonj, or political bargaining were never part of the agenda.

Ironically, factional groups supported by the state administration rejected this push for unity. Accusing participants of obstructing peace is an attempt to deflect from the state-sponsored actions that rejected a broad-based call for unification of various groups under one umbrella to be co-chaired by the two community leaders.

Conclusion and Call to Action

The decision to dissolve the Tonj Community Leadership in Juba was a voluntary, lawful step taken by Ustaz Lewis Anei Madut Kuendit to respect tenure limits. The Preparatory Committee’s actions comply fully with its mandate.

The Governor’s intervention appears driven by unverified reports, political vendettas, and self-interested advisers. Using the executive authority of Warrap State to settle local political disputes undermines the integrity of public governance.

We call upon H.E. Governor Bol Wek Agoth to:

1. Immediately retract the letter addressed to the NSS leadership.

2. Allow the Tonj Community in Juba to proceed with its scheduled elections in accordance with its established guidelines.

3. Adopt an inclusive approach to governance that fosters unity across all sections of Greater Tonj.

4. Engage all stakeholders in Tonj and listen from all sides before making administrative directives that carry the weight of law. Doing that will not just enhance the credibility of his authority but will promote fairness and justice.

Signed on behalf of Greater Tonj Community Union

Andrew Kuac Mayol Gai
Chairperson

Date: 21 August 2026

text:
Becky Akuindiik Abiem: The Slayqueen Who Traded a Gen. Maroldit Love for a Deceit and Got Her Teeth Knocked Out by Road Justice

The tale of Akuindiik Abiem is a  cautionary comedy for all Juba slayqueens who are playing around for gain. It is the tale of the desperate hyena without principle and a warning for all slayqueens dreaming of scamming an army general.

In the busy streets of Juba, where gossip moves faster than a motorbike and everyone knows everybody's business, a big drama was happening. Seven years ago, Becky Akuindiik Abiem, the girl who thought she was the smartest slayqueen in all of South Sudan, had pulled off the greatest trick ever... until her lies literally crashed into her face and knocked out her front teeth!

You see, Akuindiik was engaged to General Lual Maroldit, the former Commander of Tiger Division, a man so tough that just hearing his name made people shake in their shoes. The deal was simple: Akuindiik would finish her studies in Uganda, and after graduation, they would get married. The generous General paid for everything: school fees, rent, and pocket money that would make a government minister jealous. Life was sweet for our slayqueen!

But Akuindiik, whose moral compass was spinning like a confused chicken, had other plans. While her fiancé thought she was busy attending classes in Kampala, she was actually painting Juba red—or should I say, painting the town with lies! She secretly came back to Juba and checked into a hotel with her secret boyfriend (whose name is probably now dirt in certain circles). The family knew nothing. The General knew nothing. Only the hotel receptionist, who was probably paid well to keep quiet, knew the truth.

But our heroine wasn't satisfied with just one lie. Oh no! Like a hyena that can't resist the night's fun, Akuindiik would sneak out of her hotel room at midnight to party at nightclubs. Because apparently, cheating on a military general wasn't risky enough—she needed to add extra danger to her already crazy cocktail of bad choices!

One early morning, as she was coming back from the nightclub (probably drunk and panicking to get back to the hotel before her clueless boyfriend woke up and come back from the night work), she pushed her boda-boda rider to drive like a race car driver. She needed to be back before sunrise!

That's when karma decided to step in. Arriving at Tombura road junction, near the University of Jama Juba, with star trek movie drone speed, the motorcycle crashed, and Akuindiik's face met the tarmac road in a spectacular show of poetic justice epic. Her front teeth? Gone. The teeth vanished without trace of one tooth till date of writing. Her gum turned into gravel decorations on the Juba road. It was the new beauty in the making.

When the passerby recognized the bloody face of "General Maroldit's fiancée," chaos broke out! One phone call and the General, who was probably enjoying his morning tea, before heading to the work, was nearly choked when he heard the news. "But she's in Uganda!" he insisted on a phone conversation. Maroldit did not believe Akuindiik got into an accident in Juba until his bodyguards went to the scene and confirmed the unbelievable truth: his "studious" fiancée was actually a nighttime party animal running around Juba!

Being a gentleman, general Maroldit swallowed the saliva and arranged for her hospital treatment and even chartered a plane to send her abroad for the best medical care. He replaced her teeth with the finest fake ones money could buy—though nothing could replace the holes in her credibility. But when the wounds healed and the new teeth sparkled, the General delivered the final blow: "I am not marrying a woman whose teeth are shinier than her character."

Today, Akuindiik walks the streets of Juba with her fancy new teeth and an even fancier reputation—a warning for every girl who thinks she can outsmart a Tiger Commander. Because in South Sudan, we say: "You can run from your problems, but you can't outrun a boda-boda accident!"

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

text:
The Watchdog Press Administration Will Not Be Silenced by Tribalism or Political Patronage: Response to Slay Queen Becky Abiem Akeen 

Dear side chick of PS Akol Santo and Mrs tribal journalist of Gogrial, Madame Becky Akuindik Abiem or whatever name you choose to use you have lost the argument to the core.

Your article claims that “the Presidency is treated as a highly respected national institution” and that citizens should avoid “mockery, sensationalism, or personal attacks.” Yet you appear to apply those principles selectively. If respect for institutions is genuinely your concern, then apply the same standard to everyone, including powerful officials and their associates.

You also wrote that “criticism is part of democracy, but it should be constructive, factual, and respectful.” We agree. But criticism of the government, the President, or public officials does not become irresponsible merely because it is uncomfortable. A free press is not supposed to protect the powerful from scrutiny; it is supposed to ensure that power is questioned.

Your attempt to invoke the Ministry of ICT and Postal Services, the National Communication Authority, and the Media Authority against platforms you dislike raises an even more fundamental question: Are you genuinely defending responsible journalism, or are you asking state institutions to silence journalism that exposes people you politically favor?

And here is another question: If the facts published by Watchdog Press are false, why not challenge the specific facts with evidence instead of portraying the entire platform as “irresponsible” and “abusive”?

A second question is unavoidable: Why demand dignity and protection for those in power while ignoring the dignity of ordinary citizens who depend on independent media to expose corruption, abuse, incompetence, and misuse of public resources?

The Mighty Watchdog Press has become a voice for people who often have no access to powerful offices, expensive lawyers, or government platforms. You may disagree with its tone or some of its publications, but attempting to discredit the entire platform because it scrutinizes powerful figures is intellectually dishonest.

You wrote that citizens must “promote a culture of responsible communication.” Absolutely. But responsible communication also means distinguishing between legitimate criticism and deliberate attempts to intimidate journalists into silence.

If a publication contains factual errors, produce evidence and demand a correction. If it contains defamation, pursue the lawful remedies available. But do not disguise political protectionism as a campaign for responsible journalism.

And Madam Becky, if your loyalty is to truth rather than to personalities, then let truth be your standard, even when it embarrasses your friends, allies, patrons, or political beneficiaries.

The Watchdog Press does not need to be perfect to deserve protection. It only needs the freedom to question those who wield public power.

South Sudan does not need journalists who become unofficial defenders of powerful individuals. It needs journalists courageous enough to ask difficult questions, including questions about the President, ministers, advisers, security officials, and everyone else who exercises public authority.

You can criticize Watchdog Press. You can challenge its facts. You can demand accountability. But you cannot redefine accountability as disrespect simply because the questions are uncomfortable.

The louder the attempt to intimidate independent voices becomes, the more necessary those voices become.

The Mighty Watchdog Press must remain a watchdog, not a lapdog. And no amount of tribal loyalty, political patronage, intimidation, or institutional pressure should turn the press into a shield for the powerful.

To this end, we urged you to maintain our respect for you because of your responsible uncles and Aguok Community leader Hon. Natelina Aweng Abior whom we profoundly respect for their national responsibilities where they made historical sacrifices during liberation struggle and after the Independence of South Sudan. Please be informed that your failure to acknowledge your terrible mistake and issue an apology to Watchdog Press, we will begin to introduce you to the public in pieces right away from those years which you know very well. You have invited us to overhaul you in the eyes of the public as a response or reasonable punishment to your unprovoked attempt to sellout the Mighty Watchdog Press. Thank God we have 90% data of who you are.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

Update on the Situation of Ill Sultan Aduol Arol Aduol in Juba

We have received further information regarding the health and treatment situation of the elderly Sultan Aduol Arol Aduol, whose condition continues to cause serious concern among his relatives, community members, and well-wishers.

This update comes amid the recent articles published by the Watchdog Press Facebook page and the subsequent response from the Gregory Vasilis Facebook page. The purpose of this statement is to provide a further account of the situation and to highlight the concerns being raised by those seeking assistance for the sick elderly Sultan Aduol Arol.

Deputy First Lady Gregory Vasilis is still refusing to provide the financial assistance requested by individuals who have approached him on behalf of Sultan Aduol Arol Aduol. Those who have gone to him to plead for assistance have instead been told to leave or face arrest and imprisonment.

During these encounters, Gregory Vasilis expressed deep personal resentment toward his maternal relatives. He recalled that following the death of his late father, Vasilli, members of his immediate maternal family, particularly the Pacheer clan, abandoned him and his siblings when they were young. He said that it was only through the intervention of the late General Salva Mathok Gengdit that their difficult situation at the time was addressed and they became a successful powerful family today.

However, regardless of any historical family grievances or disagreements, the present situation concerns the health and wellbeing of an elderly and seriously ill man. Personal disputes should not become a barrier to humanitarian assistance, particularly when the individual in question is in urgent need of medical treatment.

Gregory Vasilis has repeatedly told people who approach him on Sultan Aduol Arol Aduol’s behalf that the Sultan Aduol will not survive, regardless of whether they continue pleading with him or even approach his sister for assistance. Such statements are deeply troubling and raise serious moral and humanitarian questions.

Gregory Vasilis has also said that the only assistance he can afford at the moment is a ticket to enable Sultan Aduol Arol Aduol to return home. Meaning he wish Sultan Aduol Arol is return back home to die there slowly.

The central question, therefore, is not about political allegiance, family history, or personal disagreements. It is whether an elderly and sick citizen should be denied timely medical assistance when his condition requires urgent attention.

We call upon all concerned parties, community leaders, relatives, government officials, humanitarian actors, and well-wishers to put the welfare of Sultan Aduol Arol Aduol above personal differences. If there are disagreements surrounding the matter, they should be addressed separately without compromising the Sultan’s access to urgent medical care.

An elderly person's life should never become a bargaining tool in a dispute rooted in past grievances. At this critical moment, compassion, humanity, and the preservation of life must come first.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

text:
Subject: Appeal for the Removal of Ustaz Morris Mabior Awikjok as Secretary of the Greater Tonj Peace Committee

To: The Chairman and Members of the Greater Tonj Peace Committee

From: The Luackoth Community and Its Youth Groups
Authored by: Dut Mapal, Luackoth Community Representative

Formal Appeal

We, the Luackoth Community and its youth groups, respectfully submit this formal appeal calling for the removal of Ustaz Morris Mabior Awikjok from his position as Secretary of the Greater Tonj Peace Committee.

We recognize and appreciate the important role played by the Greater Tonj Peace Committee in promoting peace, reconciliation, coexistence, and unity among communities. However, we are deeply concerned about remarks attributed to Ustaz Morris Mabior Awikjok concerning the Luackoth Community and the academic achievement of Professor Dr. Ramzy Muorwel Matueny, whom the community recognizes as its first PhD holder.

In particular, we are concerned by his reference to the Luackoth Community as “Palestinians” in connection with the community's celebration of Professor Dr. Ramzy Muorwel Matueny's achievement. We consider such language inappropriate and inconsistent with the responsibility entrusted to the secretary of a peace committee.

A person serving in a peacebuilding institution is expected to exercise restraint, neutrality, sensitivity, and respect toward all communities. Public remarks that communities perceive as derogatory, divisive, or inflammatory can undermine the very trust that peacebuilding institutions are established to create.

The Luackoth Community has consistently sought cordial relations with neighboring communities and has participated in peacebuilding and reconciliation efforts. We therefore strongly object to language that, in our view, unfairly labels or compares our community to a conflict-ridden society.

Concern Regarding Neutrality

The Secretary of the Greater Tonj Peace Committee holds a position that requires impartiality and confidence from all participating communities. Where members of a community believe that the secretary has publicly used language that demeans or alienates them, the credibility of the committee itself can be affected.

We therefore believe that the matter should not be dismissed as a personal disagreement or an ordinary social-media dispute. It deserves serious consideration because the conduct of peace committee officials directly affects public confidence in the peace process.

Our Demands

We respectfully call upon the Chairman and members of the Greater Tonj Peace Committee to:

1. Review the conduct and remarks attributed to Ustaz Morris Mabior Awikjok.
2. Take appropriate and decisive action regarding his continued service as Secretary of the Greater Tonj Peace Committee.
3. Consider his removal from the position if the committee determines that his conduct has compromised the neutrality and confidence required of the office.
4. Issue an appropriate public statement or apology to the Luackoth Community and other affected parties.
5. Reaffirm the committee's commitment to neutrality, mutual respect, inclusion, and peaceful coexistence among all communities.

A Final Recommendation to Ustaz Morris Mabior Awikjok

Ustaz Morris Mabior Awikjok should seriously reflect on whether remaining in this position continues to serve the interests of peace and his own community.

If he is not desperate for something material or personal from this committee, he should consider stepping aside voluntarily and continue serving and supporting his community through other meaningful means. Community service is not confined to a particular title, position, or committee. A person can contribute greatly to his people without holding an official position, particularly when remaining in that position has become a source of mistrust and controversy.

Stepping aside would not necessarily represent defeat. On the contrary, it could demonstrate maturity, responsibility, and a genuine commitment to preserving peace and community relations.

We therefore urge the Greater Tonj Peace Committee to handle this matter with seriousness, fairness, and urgency. The credibility of any peace institution depends on its ability to maintain neutrality and ensure that every community feels respected and represented.

We hope that this appeal will receive due consideration and that appropriate action will be taken to restore trust, dignity, and confidence in the Greater Tonj peacebuilding process.

Sincerely,
Dut Mapal, the most regarded Youth Leader from Tonj East County of Warrap State.
Luackoth Community Representative

text:
Salary Is a Right, Not a Political Bargaining Chip

Recently, a Member of Parliament from Northern Bahr El Ghazal State made a public statement warning that the people of Aweil, and South Sudan more broadly, will not vote in the upcoming elections unless the government clears their outstanding salaries, which have gone unpaid for two years.

While the demand for unpaid salaries is entirely legitimate, the way it has been framed is problematic and lack civil duty conscience. Tying salary payment to electoral participation or political support reduces a fundamental right to a transactional bargain. This approach is not only politically shallow but also undermines the very principles of citizenship and accountability.

First, salary is an earned right, not a reward for loyalty. Government employees work for their pay. Their salaries are not gifts from the president or any political party. They are legal entitlements backed by employment contracts and public service obligations. No worker should have to chant political slogans or pledge allegiance before receiving what they have already earned. To suggest otherwise is to accept that salaries depend on political favor, which is precisely the kind of system that has enabled the current crisis. It give political elites, who are perpetrators, right over what is not their, I think the MP is not well informed.

Second, elections are a constitutional duty, not a bargaining tool.
Threatening to boycott elections unless salaries are paid confuses two separate issues. Elections belong to the people and the nation; they are not personal property that public employees can offer or withhold in exchange for back pay. Using them as leverage weakens the democratic process and sends the wrong message, that citizens' political participation is for sale, rather than a sovereign right. In elections, all citizens can vote whether they are employed or not.

Third, the real failure is governance, not political support. Two years without salary is a profound failure of state responsibility. Those responsible, whether in executive offices, finance ministries, or oversight bodies, must be held accountable. But accountability requires clear, principled demands. Citizens should say: “Pay us because we worked, and because the law requires it.” Not: “Pay us, and then we will support you.” The former is a demand for justice; the latter is a negotiation that dignifies injustice.

Finally, rights and choices must remain separate. A salary is a right. A vote is a right. Political support is a free choice. None of these should be traded for another. When we mix them, we weaken all three. We give the government an excuse to treat salaries as political favors, and we reduce ourselves to bargaining for what is already ours.

The people of South Sudan deserve their salaries, fully and without delay. But they also deserve a political culture where rights are claimed with dignity, not offered as currency. The cry for justice must be clear, firm, and principled, not conditional, not transactional, and never dependent on a political slogan of Oyee as MP put it.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

text:
Dear Hon. Awel Deng Juac, Madam Divorced Queen of Labata: My Jaw is on the Floor!

Oh my goodness, Allah-Kam, Awel Deng Juach! Should I laugh until my ribs crack or cry until my tears form a new river in Juba? Eeh! So you really said "bye-bye" to your husband Agel Riing Machar, again? And then, instead of keeping this sacred family matter between you and your pillow, you ran to your Facebook and TikTok army and tell them to shout louds, "AWEL HAS DEVORCED AGEL!" like you are announcing a presidential election result! Wah! This is like someone falling into a muddy puddle and then deciding to roll in it again just for the entertainment of onlookers!

Listen, my dear, your two big mistakes are as rotten as a fish left in the sun for three days, and then you decided to film yourself vomiting it online for the whole world to see after eating it. First, you divorced Agel (again??), and second, you turned your marital drama into a Netflix series for your followers. What you do not realize is that even your own family members are now scratching their heads so hard they might go bald, asking, "Awel, what is wrong with you?" It seems shame has packed its bags, left your body, and emigrated to another country permanently!

Remember, when Agel found you and married you, you had already divorced Mony Bor before him, isn't it? Sister, are you collecting divorce certificates like they are football medals? What will you do with all these marriage and divorce papers, create a beautiful wallpaper frame for your living room so that visitors can admire your "achievements of broken marriages"? Yaa Allah!

Now, you are running after Bibi Ali, that old man with more wives than he has teeth, all because of his money! Just because money without other benefits including the healthy dick you have abandoned! You left Agel, the man who loved you like his own eyes, who would have fought a lion for you, just for someone's grandfather who already has wives scattered everywhere like maize grains after a harvest! Are you really sane, or has the Juba sun fried your brain? You better wait for Dr. Riek Machar to be released soon and beg him to marry you or maintain your secret love affairs with Hon. Mayiik Ayii Deng instead of useless Bibi Ali. Or you alternatively marry tycoon Kiir Gai Thiep or Governor Bol Wek Agoth if you only want an Aguok man. Do that please!

You have convinced yourself that leaving the wonderful life with the father of your children was a smart move. But girl, that is like leaving a cold, refreshing Coke for warm, dirty tap water! And telling your facebook army to share everything on social media? That was like climbing to the top of Jebel Kujur and screaming your secrets through a loudspeaker for everyone in South Sudan to hear!

First mistake: divorce. Second mistake: social media. And your third secret plan? Becoming a wife number something to that useless businessman from your village who has more wives than he has hair on his head! This is a deadly sin that will follow you like your shadow for eternity. Even your grandchildren will hear this story and laugh so hard they'll choke on their porridge! These are mistakes only someone who grew up in a village without TV and thinks "urban life" means owning a smartphone with TikTok can make!

Nobody believes you keep doing these embarrassing things one after another like a broken record, skrrrt, skrrrt, divorce, skrrrt, divorce! You have tied this shame to your name like a permanent necklace made of cow dung, dear!

Let me tell you straight, sister: you have stabbed yourself with your own spoon, and then twisted it for good measure! You have left God's path and you are now dancing with the devil in high heels. Even yourself, you know this in your heart when you are alone at night, staring at your phone screen, wondering, "What have I done?"

I can tell you honestly, even if you have money, even if you are happy now (are you really?), even if your new man promises you the moon, the stars, and a lifetime supply of chicken's milks, and even if you have secret powers, my dear Hon. Awel, take this from me: yin chi thaar gud atueldu rot (you know what I mean!). Start accepting that you have lost life's real meaning. You are destroying yourself slowly, like termites eating a chair from the inside out! Your village-girl antics have made God angry, and He is shaking His head at you so hard He might get whiplash! Just wait for abomination. What you did to Agel and those innocent children is something God will remember like we remember our first kiss—forever!

Madam Awel, all these years I heard stories about you and other people. I thought you had some sense, but now I know you are the most silliest, most dramatic Dinka woman I have ever heard of in my entire life! Simply put, you have signed a deal with the devil without reading the tiny, invisible fine print. You have made God angry with your soap opera drama. You have willingly thrown yourself under the bus—and then asked the driver to reverse and run over you again, sister Awel!

Sister Awel, in Dinka tradition, a mother of three doesn't remarry, she retires from marriage like an old football referee! Not only that, in Dinka Society, a divorced woman cannot be allowed to get married again, she is supposed to feel ashamed. She is supposed to sit down, drink tea, and reflect, so that she should not set cultural precedents like breaking Olympic records! Now you are running after Bibi Ali, If he is serious, tell him in advance to prepare for an accepting potential divorce certificate from you in order to avoid a stroke later. because I'm convinced your marriage vows come with an expiry date shorter than Saudi milk in Juba stores! You collect husbands like phone numbers, but none survive! "Till death do us part" for you means "till boredom or someone richer appears!"

Yaa Allah, what a world!

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

text:
OPEN LETTER TO H.E. GENERAL SALVA KIIR MAYARDIT

President of the Republic of South Sudan

Subject: URGENT APPEAL FOR THE RELEASE OF DETAINEES HELD IN CONNECTION WITH THE ARC INVESTIGATION

Date: 10th August 2026

Your Excellency,

We, the families and concerned relatives of the remaining detainees at the Blue House, respectfully appeal to Your Excellency to intervene personally and bring an end to their prolonged detention without charge or appearance before a competent court.

We fully support the investigation of any alleged financial wrongdoing involving African Resources Corporation (ARC), crude oil-for-infrastructure arrangements, and public resources. Those responsible for any wrongdoing should account for their actions before the law.

However, an investigation must be based on individual evidence and individual responsibility. No citizen should remain in detention merely because he is associated with a broader investigation.

Your Excellency, some of these detainees have now spent six to nearly nine months in detention without being formally charged or presented before a competent court.

This is deeply concerning.

We also respectfully remind Your Excellency that you directed that the investigation be expedited within 30 days, that persons found not implicated be released, and that those against whom sufficient evidence exists be taken to court.

That 30-day period has now expired, yet some remain in detention.

We therefore respectfully ask: Why should your own directive not be implemented?

If there is evidence against any detainee, let that evidence be presented before a court.

If there is no evidence, let the person go home.

The ARC investigation should follow the evidence

If the investigation concerns crude oil-for-infrastructure funds, accountability should follow the complete contractual and financial chain.

The relevant former officials of the Ministries of Justice, Finance and Planning, Roads and Bridges, Petroleum, the Office of the President, as well as relevant officials of the Bank of South Sudan, contractors and technical officials who authorised, supervised, certified or paid for the relevant contracts should be examined where appropriate.

ARC itself should account for:

the contracts it received; the resources or payments it received; the work it performed; and how those resources were utilised.

The proper principle should be simple:

Follow the contract. Follow the money. Follow the work. Follow the evidence.

That is how a credible investigation should be conducted.

The investigation must not become indefinite detention

We are also deeply concerned by allegations concerning the reported US$3.5 million investigation fee and claims of a possible financial interest in funds recovered.

If these allegations are accurate, they deserve independent scrutiny.

An investigation into public corruption must be conducted solely in the public interest. Investigators should have no financial incentive to secure particular outcomes.

Your Excellency, the families are not asking that anyone who committed an offence be protected.

We are asking for equal application of the law.

Those against whom there is evidence should face court.

Those against whom there is no evidence should be released.

Your Excellency, South Sudan needs peace

As the country approaches the December 2026 general elections, South Sudan needs reconciliation, confidence, and political stability.

The continued detention of former government officials without charge is creating deep anxiety among their families, communities, and political constituencies.

Keeping people in detention without trial does not strengthen the state; it weakens confidence in the state.

Your Excellency, releasing individuals against whom no evidence exists, would not mean abandoning the fight against corruption.

It would demonstrate that South Sudan can distinguish between investigation and punishment, accusation and evidence, and political disagreement and criminal responsibility.

We therefore humbly appeal to Your Excellency to:

Immediately review the cases of all remaining detainees;

Release those against whom the investigation has established no evidence; and

Direct that anyone against whom credible evidence exists be formally charged and brought before a competent court without further delay.

The remaining detainees are:

1. Hon. Dr. Marial Dongrin Ater
2. Amb. Ajing Deng Ajing
3. Maj. Gen. (PSC) Dominic Juk Chom
4. Hon.Eng. Deng Lual Wol
5. Hon. Simon Akuei Deng
6. Hon. Eng. John Khot Chol
7. Hon. Moses Makur Deng
8. Dr. Chan Andrea Chan
9. Mr. Majok Thiel Koch
10. Mr. Bol Malang Ngong

Your Excellency,

The families are not asking for special treatment.

They are asking for the law to be applied.

They are asking that detention does not become a substitute for trial and that an investigation does not become an indefinite punishment.

Release those who have been cleared.
Charge those against whom there is evidence.
Take the cases to court.
Let justice not detention determine guilt.

At this important moment in our nation’s history, justice can become the bridge to peace.

Respectfully,

Representatives of the Families of the Detainees.

Juba, Republic of South Sudan

text:
The Core Revenue Collection Contradiction: Who Pays, Who Is Exempt?

In July 2026, Gen. Pieng Deng Kuol was appointed to chair a High-Level Committee on Economic Reform mandated, among other things, to strengthen and reform national revenue collection. On 27 July 2026, the Committee met in Nimule, Eastern Equatoria State, with representatives of clearing agencies, commercial banks, customs authorities and security institutions. During the meeting, the Chairperson reportedly emphasised that increasing government revenue was a national priority and called for greater coordination among institutions responsible for revenue collection. He further directed that suppliers, contractors and subcontractors comply with their tax obligations before their goods are cleared.

The objective of improving domestic revenue mobilisation is neither controversial nor unreasonable. A state cannot provide security, pay its civil servants, maintain public institutions or finance development without a functioning and equitable fiscal system. The problem, however, arises when the government demands strict compliance from some taxpayers while leaving unresolved questions about the fiscal treatment of other territories administered or financed by the same state.

This raises a fundamental question that the Ministry of Finance and Planning, the South Sudan National Revenue Authority (NRA) and the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform should answer publicly:

Does Abyei form part of South Sudan’s national fiscal and revenue-collection system, and if so, why is its treatment apparently different from that imposed on taxpayers at places such as Nimule?

Since the establishment of the Abyei Special Administrative Area by the Government of South Sudan in July 2015, questions have repeatedly arisen concerning the collection, administration and remittance of non-oil revenues generated in or through Abyei. If revenues generated within an area administered and supported by the Government of South Sudan are outside the oversight of the national revenue system, the government owes the public a clear legal and fiscal explanation.

This is not merely a political question. It is a question of fiscal equality, institutional accountability and the rule of law.

A trader operating at Nimule is expected to comply with customs requirements, taxation and other government charges before goods can enter the country. Contractors and suppliers are instructed to meet their tax obligations before their transactions can proceed. Yet if another area benefiting from the political, administrative or financial support of the Republic of South Sudan is permitted to operate outside the same national revenue architecture, taxpayers are entitled to ask why.

The concern becomes even more serious when the person responsible for leading a national economic-reform initiative is politically and administratively associated with an area whose fiscal relationship with the national government remains unclear.

Gen. Pieng Deng Kuol’s appointment therefore creates an obvious perception of a conflict of interest, irrespective of his personal intentions. A national revenue-reform committee must be seen to apply one standard across the country. Its credibility depends not only on what it demands from taxpayers but also on whether its leadership is prepared to subject every territory, institution and political constituency to the same fiscal rules.

The issue should therefore not be reduced to an accusation against the Ngok Dinka community or the people of Abyei. Ordinary citizens in Abyei should not be blamed for decisions made by political and administrative authorities. The real issue is the governance of public revenue and whether national fiscal institutions have equal authority throughout territories administered, funded or claimed by the Republic of South Sudan.

If Abyei has a special legal or constitutional fiscal status that exempts it from the ordinary national revenue framework, the Government of South Sudan should publish the legal instrument establishing that exemption and explain precisely what revenues are excluded, why they are excluded and who has authority to collect them.

If no such exemption exists, then the NRA should have a clear mandate to exercise appropriate revenue oversight in Abyei in accordance with South Sudanese law.

Anything less creates a two-tier fiscal system: one in which ordinary traders, businesses, contractors and civil servants are expected to finance the state while certain politically sensitive areas remain outside effective national revenue oversight.

That is precisely the kind of contradiction that can destroy public confidence in economic reform.

There is also a broader fiscal question that cannot be ignored. If the Government of South Sudan continues to allocate public funds to support the administration and operations of the Abyei Special Administrative Area, while revenues generated there are not transparently incorporated into the national fiscal framework, the public deserves to know the financial rationale.

How much does the national government allocate to the Abyei Administration each financial year? What revenues are collected within the area? Which institution collects them? Where are those revenues deposited? Are they reported to the national Treasury? And what legal framework governs their collection and expenditure?

These are basic questions of public financial management, not questions of ethnicity.

The same principle must apply to the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform itself. Economic reform cannot mean increasing the tax burden on already struggling businesses while leaving politically protected revenue streams outside the national system. Nor can reform succeed if national institutions are perceived as instruments for extracting resources from some communities while protecting others from the same obligations.

The Government therefore needs to resolve this contradiction openly.

First, the Ministry of Finance and Planning should issue a comprehensive public clarification on the fiscal and revenue status of the Abyei Special Administrative Area.

Second, the National Revenue Authority should clarify whether it has legal jurisdiction to administer and audit non-oil revenue collected in Abyei and, if not, identify the legal basis for that limitation.

Third, the Government should publish the annual budgetary allocations made to the Abyei Administration and provide an account of how those funds are financed.

Fourth, the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform should disclose whether Abyei falls within the scope of its revenue-reform mandate and, if it does, explain what measures are being taken to bring revenue collection there into the national fiscal framework.

Finally, Gen. Pieng Deng should address the perceived conflict of interest created by his position. If the fiscal arrangements governing Abyei place him in a position where he cannot objectively advocate for the same revenue standards nationwide, he should consider recusing himself from matters directly concerning Abyei—or, where the conflict is substantive and unavoidable, stepping aside from the committee’s leadership.

South Sudan does not need a revenue system based on political privilege. It needs a system based on law, transparency, equality and accountability.

The Government cannot credibly tell citizens at Nimule, Juba, Wau, Malakal or elsewhere that everyone must pay while failing to provide a convincing explanation of whether the same principle applies in Abyei.

Revenue reform must therefore begin with a simple principle:

No taxpayer should be compelled to carry a burden from which politically connected constituencies are exempt.

If the Government genuinely intends to reform South Sudan’s economy, it must first eliminate the perception that there are two fiscal systems—one for ordinary taxpayers and another for politically protected territories.

Until that contradiction is resolved, the public has every reason to question whether the current revenue-reform programme represents genuine institutional reform or merely another mechanism for extracting more resources from citizens without establishing equal accountability at the centre.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future
