MY APPEAL TO WATCHDOG PRESS: LET US JUDGE ECONOMIC REFORM BY RESULTS

I have followed Watchdog Press for a considerable time and have appreciated many of its publications on governance, accountability, public resources and South Sudan’s economic challenges.

However, after reading the recent discussion concerning the appointment of Gen. Pieng Deng Kuol as Chairperson of the High-Level Committee on Economic Reform, I believe there is another perspective that deserves consideration.

I agree that questions about revenue collection, including the fiscal and administrative treatment of Abyei, are legitimate. The Government should be able to explain clearly how revenues are collected, who has authority to collect them, where they are deposited, and what legal framework governs them.

But I respectfully disagree with the conclusion that these unresolved questions automatically make Gen. Pieng Deng ineligible or incapable of leading a national economic-reform committee.

Let us separate two issues:

1. What is the legal and fiscal status of Abyei?
2. Can Gen. Pieng Deng objectively perform his national responsibility and deliver economic reform?

The first question should be answered by the Government, Ministry of Finance and Planning, National Revenue Authority and the applicable laws.

The second should be answered by Gen. Pieng Deng’s conduct and performance in office—not simply by his geographical or historical association.

I have personally followed Gen. Pieng Deng’s public-service journey for many years. I first became familiar with his role during the liberation period, including his involvement around Gogrial and Kuajok, and later encountered him professionally in 2015 when I was serving as an IGP.

I mention this for context, not because I have any personal interest in his appointment.

I am William Madeng Kher Madeng. I am neither a relative nor a political associate of Gen. Pieng Deng. I have no personal or financial interest in his appointment. Indeed, he may not even know that I exist.

My position is simple:

Give him an opportunity to serve, but watch him closely.

If he is responsible for increasing domestic revenue, then let us examine the revenue figures.

Watch the customs collections.

Watch tax compliance.

Watch whether leakages are reduced.

Watch expenditure.

Watch whether politically sensitive areas receive the same scrutiny as ordinary taxpayers.

And most importantly, watch the results.

I was encouraged by initiatives associated with his team concerning fuel pricing and efforts to reduce unnecessary costs. Whether such measures ultimately succeed should be determined by evidence and results.

South Sudan urgently needs economic reform. Increasing domestic revenue, reducing financial leakages, improving public financial management and strengthening institutions are difficult tasks. Anyone attempting to change the system will face criticism, particularly from interests that may benefit from the existing system.

That is why the reformer should be judged by the reform.

I also want to make one important distinction: questions about Abyei’s revenue administration should not become an accusation against the Ngok Dinka community or ordinary citizens of Abyei. The issue is institutional accountability—not ethnicity.

If Abyei has a special legal fiscal arrangement, let the Government explain it publicly.

If it does not, let the appropriate national institutions apply the law.

The same standard should apply everywhere.

As someone academically connected to this subject, I am not raising this matter merely as a political observer. I hold a Bachelor’s Degree in Accounting and Finance from the University of Juba and have completed an MBA in Finance at the University of Juba.

My academic background gives me a particular interest in revenue mobilisation, taxation, public financial management and economic reform. It does not make my opinion automatically correct, but it gives me a reasonable basis to ask whether fiscal accountability is being applied consistently.

Therefore, my respectful appeal to Watchdog Press is:

Do not stop watching Gen. Pieng Deng. Watch him even more closely.

If he succeeds, let the results speak.

If he fails, let the evidence speak.

But let us give him the opportunity to prove himself.

South Sudan does not need economic reform based on personalities, ethnicity or political privilege. It needs reform based on law, transparency, equal standards, accountability and measurable results.

Give the reform a chance. Give the committee an opportunity. Then let the results speak.

Respectfully,
William Madeng Kher Madeng

text:
Uganda and Tanzania Strengthen Economic Partnership Through EACOP

Uganda is poised to contribute significantly to Tanzania's economic growth through the construction of the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP), a 1,443-kilometre heated pipeline stretching from Uganda's oil fields in Hoima to Chongoleani near the Port of Tanga in Tanzania.

The pipeline is designed to transport up to 246,000 barrels of crude oil per day for export through Tanzania's Indian Ocean coastline. With more than 1,100 kilometres of the pipeline traversing Tanzanian territory, the country is expected to benefit from transit revenues, employment opportunities, infrastructure development, and increased economic activity along the pipeline corridor and around the Port of Tanga.

In many respects, Uganda's emerging oil industry is also creating substantial economic opportunities for Tanzania, reinforcing the strategic economic partnership between the two neighboring countries.

A Cry for Justice: The Blood Price of Governorship in Lakes State

By our Lakes State Correspondent

We demand the immediate arrest of Mabor Machar Puot and the removal of Governor Madhang Majok Meen, whose tenure is stained by ritual sacrifice and nepotistic violence.

Juba, South Sudan – We write this with heavy hearts and trembling hands, not as political adversaries, but as grieving families and aggrieved citizens. We are sounding an urgent alarm over the descent of leadership in Lakes State into a realm of darkness, where the lives of innocent youths are traded for political power, and where the law has been rendered mute by the protection of the powerful.

The facts are clear and deeply disturbing. On 19th January 2026, President Salva Kiir appointed Gen. Madhang Majok Meen as the Governor of Lakes State. However, the path to that appointment was not paved with merit or public will, but, as widely known within the community, through the dark arts of witchcraft, spiritual manipulation, and family connections.

We, the families of the victims, can no longer remain silent while the blood of our children cries out from the ground.

The Victims: Two Brothers, One Brutal Fate

We specifically bring to the nation’s attention the horrific murder of two young brothers from the Reech family:

1. Makou Deng Reech, aged 17
2. Sebit Deng Reech, aged 15

These vibrant young men were not victims of a communal clash or a misunderstanding. They were deliberately killed by Mabor Machar Puot, the immediate brother of Akol Machar Puot, the wife of Governor Madhang. Their lives were taken not for revenge or theft, but for a more sinister purpose: ritual sacrifice as instructed by Gen. Madhang

It is an open secret in the community that these killings were orchestrated to satisfy the "gods" and spiritual forces that Governor Madhang relied upon to secure his gubernatorial seat. The Reech brothers are not the first casualties of this macabre ambition. Previously, under the direct guidance of the Governor, Mabor Machar Puot was used to murder over three family members of Akolda Lueth from the Pagok Section of Duony Payam, Cueibet County—all in the name of appeasing the spirits for political advancement in his previous appointment as governor of defunct Gok State.

A State Held Hostage by Witchcraft

The situation has deteriorated beyond mere gossip. It has become a governance crisis. Today, it is a known fact that no government decision is taken in Lakes State without the prior approval of Governor Madhang’s witchcraft powers. A Governor who bows to spirits rather than the constitution is a danger to the Republic of South Sudan. His reliance on ritual killings has created a culture of impunity where human life is devalued, and the rule of law is treated as an inconvenience.

Despite the public nature of these crimes and the clear evidence pointing to Mabor Machar Puot, he remains a free man. This is not a failure of the police; it is an act of direct protection by the Governor. Instead of handing over his brother-in-law to face the full wrath of the law, Governor Madhang has chosen to shield the killer. By doing so, he is sending a terrifying message: The lives of the citizens of Lakes State are forfeit, and the state apparatus exists only to serve the Governor and his family.

We, the community watchdogs, are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for the justice that is the right of every South Sudanese citizen. We call upon the following authorities to act immediately:

1. To the National Ministry of Justice and the South Sudan Police Service: Arrest Mabor Machar Puot without delay. He must be held accountable for the murders of Makou Deng Reech, Sebit Deng Reech, and the family members of Akolda Lueth. He must face prosecution to the full extent of the law.

2. To H.E. President Salva Kiir and the National Government: We demand a thorough investigation into the conduct of Governor Madhang Majok Meen. A leader who sponsors, enables, or encourages ritual murder to ascend to power is unfit to govern. We call for his immediate removal and for him to face a tribunal for complicity in these heinous crimes.

3. To the International Community and Human Rights Organizations: We urge you to observe the situation in Lakes State. The suppression of justice in this case is a violation of the most fundamental human rights—the right to life and the right to due process.

The blood of the Reech brothers and the other victims is on the hands of the Governor. We cannot allow the dead to cry for justice in vain. We call on all peace-loving citizens, civil society organizations, and the international community to stand up for justice.

We demand accountability. We demand that the weapons of violence and witchcraft be replaced by the instruments of law and order. We demand Justice for Makou and Sebit.

text:
A Crisis of Institutional Protocol in the Eyes of Influential Leader Adut Salva Kiir Mayardit: Police Promotions, Ministerial Authority, and the Rule of Law in South Sudan

Recent developments within the South Sudan National Police Service have raised serious questions about institutional discipline, administrative procedures, and the relationship between the leadership of the Ministry of Interior and the Inspector General of Police.

There are growing concerns that the Inspector General of Police, Gen. Saed Chawul Lom, has once again taken unilateral decisions regarding promotions within the police service. This is the second occasion on which large-scale, or what some observers consider "inflated," promotions have been announced without sufficient regard for the established administrative procedures and protocols expected to govern promotions within a professional security institution.

The central concern is not merely the number of officers promoted, but the process through which such promotions are made. In any disciplined institution, particularly a national police service, promotions are expected to follow clear criteria, including professional qualifications, training, experience, performance, seniority where applicable, and the recommendations and approvals required by the relevant authorities. When such procedures are bypassed, the credibility of the entire promotion system is called into question.

Of particular concern are cases in which some individuals who have received police ranks have not undergone the necessary police training or orientation expected of members of the police service. Such a practice raises fundamental questions about professionalism, competence, and the institutional identity of the police service. A police rank should represent more than a title; it should signify training, responsibility, discipline, experience, and readiness to perform the duties entrusted to an officer by the Republic.

The concern, therefore, extends beyond individual promotions. It touches on the broader question of whether South Sudan is building professional institutions governed by rules or institutions increasingly influenced by individual discretion.

The Importance of Ministry of Interior Protocols

The Ministry of Interior occupies a critical position within the national security architecture of South Sudan. The police service does not operate in isolation from the ministry responsible for its political and administrative oversight. Consequently, institutional decisions affecting the structure, ranks, and administration of the police should be handled through established channels.

The repeated promotions undertaken outside the expected ministerial protocols deserve serious public and institutional scrutiny.

This should not be interpreted as opposition to the promotion of deserving police officers. On the contrary, deserving officers should be promoted, recognized, and rewarded. However, promotions become problematic when questions arise regarding whether the correct procedures were followed, whether the appropriate authorities were consulted, and whether those receiving ranks possess the qualifications and professional background required for the positions they occupy.

A professional police service cannot be built on shortcuts.

Questions Concerning the Relationship Between the Minister and the IGP

Another matter that has attracted public attention is the relationship between the Inspector General of Police and the incumbent Minister of Interior, Hon. Lt. Gen. Aleu Ayieny Aleu.

There are growing concerns that the authority of the Minister has, on several occasions, been undermined by actions attributed to the Inspector General. This raises a much larger institutional question: Who ultimately provides political and administrative oversight of the national police service?

The Minister of Interior is the political head of the ministry, while the Inspector General is responsible for the professional command and administration of the police service. These roles are distinct, but they must operate within a framework of cooperation, accountability, and respect for the chain of command established by law and government policy.

A subordinate officer should not be perceived as competing with, humiliating, or overriding the authority of the political head of the institution. Likewise, ministerial authority should not be exercised in a manner that interferes with the professional responsibilities legally assigned to the police command.

The solution, therefore, is not personal confrontation but institutional clarity.

The Question of Insubordination

The strongest criticism emerging from this controversy concerns institutional insubordination.

When the Inspector General makes major decisions affecting police ranks and structures without appropriate consultation with the responsible ministry, and such conduct is repeated despite previous concerns, the matter should be examined through the appropriate governmental and legal mechanisms.

South Sudan cannot afford a situation in which senior officials interpret their positions according to personal power rather than institutional responsibility.

The history of the liberation struggle has produced leaders who sacrificed enormously for the establishment of the Republic. Gen. Aleu Ayieny Aleu, like many members of the liberation generation, has a political and historical background that commands respect. His appointment as Minister of Interior should therefore be understood within the broader framework of strengthening national institutions and advancing reforms in the security sector.

However, the legitimacy of any minister's authority must ultimately derive from the Constitution, the laws, and the structures of government—not merely from liberation credentials.

Similarly, the authority of the Inspector General must come from the law and the office he occupies, not from personal influence or political alliances.

Political Protection

There are growing concerns that certain senior figures believe they possess sufficient political influence to shield themselves from accountability within the Ministry of Interior.

The existence of such perceptions is itself troubling.

No public official should operate under the assumption that political connections make him untouchable. Neither the Minister of Interior, nor the Inspector General of Police, nor any other government official should be above institutional accountability.

South Sudan's institutions will become stronger only when public office is understood as a responsibility rather than personal authority.

Reform Requires Institutional Discipline

The reported controversy is particularly significant because the Ministry of Interior requires meaningful reform. The country needs a police service that is professional, politically neutral in its operational duties, properly trained, adequately equipped, and accountable to the law.

Reform cannot succeed if institutional procedures are repeatedly ignored.

If promotions are necessary, let them be conducted transparently. Let the relevant committees examine the qualifications of candidates. Let training requirements be respected. Let the appropriate ministry authorities participate in accordance with the law. Let deserving officers receive recognition based on merit, competence, experience, and service.

That would strengthen the police institution rather than weaken it.

The country should not create a situation in which police ranks become instruments of political patronage or personal loyalty. A rank in the National Police Service must carry professional meaning and public confidence.

A Call for Institutional Review

In light of these concerns, there is a legitimate basis for calling for an institutional review of the recent promotion decisions.

Such a review should establish:

- Whether the promotions complied with applicable laws, regulations, and Ministry of Interior procedures;
- Whether the individuals promoted possessed the necessary qualifications and police training;
- Whether the appropriate ministerial and police authorities participated in the promotion process;
- Whether previous promotion decisions followed the same procedures;
- Whether there were administrative disagreements between the Ministry of Interior and the police leadership;
- Whether any individual exercised authority beyond the powers legally assigned to his office; and
- What measures should be taken to prevent similar institutional disputes in the future.

This would not amount to undermining the police. Rather, it would strengthen the police service by ensuring that its leadership operates within a predictable and accountable institutional framework.

The Republic Must Come Before Individuals

The fundamental issue is bigger than Gen. Saed Chawul Lom, Hon. Aleu Ayieny Aleu, Gen. Kon John Akot, or any other individual mentioned in the controversy.

South Sudan must move away from a culture in which institutions are perceived through the personalities occupying them.

Ministers come and go. Inspectors General come and go. Generals come and go. Political leaders come and go. But the institutions of the Republic must remain.

If the Inspector General has acted within his lawful authority, that authority should be demonstrated through the applicable legal and administrative provisions. If he has exceeded his mandate, the appropriate authorities should address the matter through lawful institutional mechanisms.

Likewise, if the Minister of Interior has acted within his mandate, his authority should be respected. If there are disagreements between the Minister and the Inspector General, those disagreements should be resolved through government procedures rather than public confrontation, political speculation, or competing demonstrations of power.

Conclusion

The second round of controversial police promotions should not be reduced to a personal disagreement between senior government officials. It presents an opportunity for South Sudan to ask a more fundamental question: Are our security institutions governed by established rules, or are they increasingly shaped by individual discretion and political influence?

The people of South Sudan deserve a police service that commands respect because of its professionalism, not because of the rank of the individuals leading it.

Where promotion procedures have been bypassed, the matter should be investigated. Where individuals without the required professional training have been granted police ranks, the matter should be reviewed. Where ministerial authority has been disregarded, the relevant constitutional and administrative mechanisms should clarify the boundaries of authority. Where any official has exceeded his mandate, accountability should follow regardless of political connections or personal influence.

The Minister of Interior should be able to pursue his reform agenda without being undermined by subordinates, while the Inspector General should be able to perform his professional responsibilities without undue political interference. The two offices should complement one another—not compete for institutional supremacy.

Ultimately, no individual should be bigger than the institution, and no institution should be bigger than the law.

South Sudan needs disciplined leadership, professional security institutions, transparent promotion procedures, and respect for the chain of command. The country has paid too high a price to allow personal rivalries, perceived political protection, or administrative shortcuts to weaken the institutions for which generations of South Sudanese struggled.

Hon. Lt. Gen. Aleu Ayieny Aleu is being openly and disrespectfully insubordinated by Inspector General Gen. Saed Chawul Lom and his allies. Such conduct creates the perception that decisions are being driven by a narrow circle of influence rather than by the national institutions established to serve all South Sudanese. This is not the national government for which the 64 tribes of South Sudan fought and sacrificed millions of lives. National institutions must serve the entire country with professionalism, legality, and respect for the established chain of command.

The Plot to Remove Honorable Africano Mande from the Ministry of Presidential Affairs and Reinstate Honorable Mayiik Ayii Deng 

By Our Correspondent

There is a troubling scheme unfolding in Juba in recent days. Mr. Lang Deng Maluil, the Managing Director of South Sudan Pipelines at the Ministry of Petroleum, is actively campaigning to remove Hon. Africano Mande from his position as Minister of Presidential Affairs. Lang wants to replace him with his new friend and political ally Honorable Mayiik Ayii Deng. According to our reliable sources in the Government Institutions, we can confidently confirm that 70% to 80% of lobby is done.

The friendship between Lang and Mayiik has been there for quite a long time. This friendship has repeatedly brought them together for common interests, including this deal in recent months. They now share an apartment in Juba area and move around town together in Lang's car. They are inseparable companions who drink beer together and are known in the city for chasing women, including married women and so-called "slay queens," and underage females who are suffering from economic hardship in South Sudan. Their bond is built on a mutual deal, not genuine friendship. This is why they turned against General Akol Koor Kuc, a great man whom they heavily benefited from his authority when he was the most powerful DG of Blue House at that time. 

Mr. Lang has promised Mayiik that he will do everything possible to remove Africano Mande. Together, they have been meeting with influential elders and leaders, especially from the Awan Muorkwau and Apuk Lith Communities in Gogrial, to gain support for their plan.

Mayiik had concerns about his long-standing bad relationship with General Gregory Vasilis, who is the President's brother-in-law. Mayiik is also doubtful of DG Akech Tong's important role in making this lobby succeed. Lang told him not to worry, saying he himself is now a close friend of Gregory. Lang explained that Gregory loves money, and once you give him cash, all problems disappear. He promised to give Gregory money to fix Mayiik's relationship with him, just as he did for himself. And the same thing with DG Akech Tong, and our brother Akol Santo Arech will also help a lot, Lang said.

Mayiik also worried about having no updated connection with another key central player, Honorable Adut Salva Kiir. Again, Lang assured him that he and Gregory would talk to Adut and sort everything out. To build trust, Lang asked Mayiik to move into his apartment until he gets the Ministerial appointment. They now live together in Thongping.

This is not generosity from Lang. It is a clear tit-for-tat deal. Mayiik has made landmark thick words – by promising Lang that if he becomes Minister of Presidential Affairs, he will work within the President's Office to ensure Lang is appointed as Undersecretary for the Ministry of Petroleum. This position is currently held by Hon. Dr. Santino Ayuel Longar, who is Lang's senior. Lang became so excited and expressed that he will do anything possible to secure Mayiik's appointment within this August.

To Us as The True Voice of the Public: Here Is Why Mayiik Should Never Return to Office

Mayiik Ayii Deng has served as Minister of Presidential Affairs before, and his tenure was a disaster marked by corruption, mismanagement, and abuse of power. He also engineered a lot of dangerous conspiracies that brought many leaders and communities into endless confrontation up to date.

Corruption: Mayiik altered the Bahr El Ghazal road contract. The President had signed an agreement with the Chinese company Shandong Hi-speed, with the Chinese government as a partner. Mayiik changed this contract to favour his own shadow company called Shandong Nile Investment. The President was furious and publicly stated that this was why he removed Mayiik from the cabinet in 2020. The alteration resulted in sub-standard road works that were washed away by the first rains of that season. This was the first time in South Sudan's history since independence that President Kiir gave the public a reason for removing an official in his cabinet.

Mismanagement: During his time, there were serious leaks of the President's top secret and official documents. There was no respect for institutional protocols.

Abuse of Office: Mayiik used his position to sexually exploit young women. He recruited female workers into the President's office after gaining sexual favours from them. He targeted young girls from the University of Juba female hostel and also preyed on other men's wives. He slept with anyone seeking favours at J-1. Many of the women now working in the President's office were recruited during his time through such abuse.

Embezzlement: He stole state resources and manipulated the President while showing no respect for the rule of law.

Allowing Mayiik to return to the office of the President would be a grave mistake. He would finish whatever little is left of the state. South Sudan cannot afford to repeat the mistakes of the past. The people deserve better than corrupt officials who abuse their power and destroy public trust. Mayiik has seriously contributed to the ongoing division and conflicts among some leaders and communities not only in Warrap State. Mayiik is not important at all; he is a destructive human being everyone should be very careful of him.

text:
A Warning Against Turning Political Conflict into a War on the Liberators by Hon. Garang Paul Malong 

South Sudan must be extremely careful when political disagreements begin to take the form of persecution, intimidation, arrests, exile, or attacks against those who sacrificed their lives for the liberation of the country.

There are growing concerns about the treatment of former liberation fighters, veterans, and political figures who participated in the long struggle against Khartoum. Many of these men and women are now unemployed, without adequate pensions or medical support. Some are living in exile, while others are reportedly under detention or house arrest. These are people who sacrificed their youth, their families, their health, and, in many cases, their loved ones for the liberation of South Sudan.

It is therefore deeply troubling when members of the political establishment, including those close to the President, are perceived as targeting individuals connected to the liberation struggle. If such actions are taking place, they should stop immediately. South Sudan cannot afford to turn its history of liberation into a cycle of revenge and political persecution.

And let us be clear: today's political targets are not merely individuals. They are fathers, mothers, brothers, uncles, sons, and daughters of the people who fought for this country. If the generation that liberated South Sudan is systematically marginalized, persecuted, imprisoned, exiled, or deprived of basic dignity, what message are we sending to their children?

Political power is temporary. The nation belongs to all South Sudanese.

This is therefore a warning—not a threat—to Adut Salva Kiir Mayardit and to everyone exercising influence around the President: do not turn political differences into a war against people and families. Do not create a cycle of retaliation that future generations will inherit.

There is an old saying: “People who live in glass houses should not throw stones.” Those who have vulnerabilities of their own should be careful about creating a culture in which everyone begins throwing stones.

South Sudan has already suffered enough from war, division, displacement, and political violence. We cannot continue destroying one another after achieving independence from an external enemy.

The sons and daughters of the liberation struggle deserve dignity, justice, and respect—not persecution because of their political affiliations or the actions of their relatives.

The survival of South Sudan requires reconciliation, rule of law, justice, and responsible leadership. No family, regardless of its proximity to power, should be above the law; and no citizen, regardless of their political position, should be treated as an enemy simply for exercising their rights.

This is a warning for peace, not a declaration of war.

South Sudan belongs to all of us.

Hon. Garang Malong Awan
Former State Minister of youths, culture and sports
Northern Bahr el Ghazal State, Aweil

Quick Update on the Health Situation of Abdirashid Deng Alor Kuol

According to a circulating statement posted by a Facebook page named Southsudan TMZ, claiming that a senior member of the SPLM has died, it does not refer to Hon. Abdirashid Deng Alor Kuol, whose health remains in critical condition at one of the hospitals in Nairobi. Deng is not dead, although his condition remains extremely unstable after he collapsed in Juba and was urgently airlifted to Nairobi, Kenya, for specialized medical care. Till date he can't speak nor recognize people.

We are closely monitoring his health condition through multiple sources, including his colleague, Amb. Ezekiel Lol Gatkuoth, who is in direct communication with one of the attendants caring for the patient.

According to verification from our multiple sources, the Southsudan TMZ page is referring to a member of the NAS who unfortunately passed away abroad. May he rest in peace. We remain in solidarity with the family of the deceased during this difficult time.

Watchdog Press Management – Watching Your Future

My Facebook account has been disabled for 180 days.

By Journalist Emmanuel Malual 

The Press secretary in the office of president Arek Aldo Ajou is believed to have hired IT experts to disabled  my Facebook account which is a channel and Newspaper that feeds the people of South Sudan at large with up to date events.

It is unfortunate that the data and privacy has been breached by those who disabled my facebook account last Sunday using state resources.

Madam  Arek Aldo Ajou, the press secretary in the office of the president came to Nairobi in the morning and I lost my account the same day.

It was confirmed that she came  to Nairobi purposely to hunt for me and my facebook account. Interestingly,regimes come and go but the wounds which were inflicted during the regime in power will never heal.

The South Sudan government  especially the office of the president which is a symbol of National Unity has become a family and friendship playground where  interests of individuals are prioritised. 

 This office has unchecked powers over human life and a blanket cheque to the Country's resources. These resources have been used to assassinate the government critics,Journalists, civil  society as political dissents in exiles for telling the truths. Telling the truth in South Sudan is a direct death sentence because it is considered a crime against the State of South Sudan.   

The power  of dictatorships which siege the media freedom in South Sudan has given few liberators daughters and sons whose parents or families never contributed anything tangible towards the South Sudan Independence in 2011.

I am  a well trained journalist with  a lot of exposure in media  which made me to become a  political and social media commentator in South Sudan matters . I always focus on issues of corruption, Human Rights violation and good governance  across the political divides in the country. 

I have never posted or published  some hate speeches  including contents that contain rhetorical information that can create trouble in my country.

 To the best of my knowledge my facebook account was disabled because of two short stories that questioned the Press secretary Arek Aldo Ajou  intention to invite the Kenyan veteran journalist Jeff Koinange to  juba to interview President Kiir Mayardit.

My second opinion was about the press secretary Arek Aldo Ajou level of competency to serve as Press secretary in the office of president which is the highest  office that unites the nation. That office doesn't belong to the family and friends of the regimes.

It is unfortunate that the Facebook administration couldn't properly verify my articles instead of rushing to disabled my Facebook page which I view as a victory for autocratic leadership in Juba.

Statement Attributed to DG Akech Tong Aleu Denying Claims in Dr. Riek Machar's Case

"I have taken note of the remarks made by Lead Prosecutor Ajo Ony'Ohisa, which suggested that my office was responsible for the delay in approving the defense team's access to Dr. Riek Machar. That characterization is inaccurate and unfair.

I have never neglected my official duties or been absent from work. Even when I am engaged in official assignments outside my office, my deputy is authorized to handle administrative matters within the scope of his responsibilities.»

There were official communications and directives from above that informed how this matter was handled. As a public servant, I am bound by the chain of command and by my obligation to respect the confidentiality of official government communications. For that reason, I will not disclose the contents of those communications or speculate on the reasons behind them.

It is therefore inappropriate to single out my office or suggest that I independently caused the delay. I urge all parties, including Lead Prosecutor Ajo Ony'Ohisa, to present the facts accurately and avoid statements that unfairly attribute responsibility."

According to reliable sources familiar with the situation between the Judiciary and Blue House authorities, DG Akech was directed by the President's Office through President Kiir's Private Secretary, Brigadier General Akol Santo, who met with him days before these delays occurred. However, it appears that DG Akech is trying to shield Akol Santo.

In conclusion, the statement raises fresh questions about where responsibility for the delay truly lies. If DG Akech Tong Aleu insists that he acted on official directives from higher authorities, then transparency demands that the decision-making process be clarified rather than allowing blame to rest on a single office. Accountability should prevail over speculation.

1. If DG Akech Tong Aleu was acting on directives from higher authorities, who ultimately authorized the delay in granting the defense team access to Dr. Riek Machar?

2. If there were official instructions from above, why should the public accept responsibility being shifted while the identities of those who issued the directives remain undisclosed?

A Deal Born Out of Desperation: The Case of Pipeline MD Joseph Lang Deng, Whose Wife Ayor Gave Birth to Gregory's 100% White Blood Baby 

It started with a plea for help and ended with a secret that almost tore a family apart.

When NSS Officer Joseph Lang Deng Maluil was arrested at the Blue House prison in 2025, his wife had nowhere else to turn. With her husband behind bars facing serious health problems and family living bills piling up, she went to the office of the infamous brother-in-law of President Salva Kiir Mayardit, a blackhearted man commonly known as Deputy First Lady General Gregory Vasilis — a ruthless, powerful government official with influence over almost any case to beg for her husband Lang Deng's release.

What happened next changed everything in Lang Deng's social history.

Instead of offering legal guidance or give any support he could, General Gregory heartlessly demanded sexual favors in exchange for helping Lang Deng Maluil to be released. Cornered and desperate, Lang's wife, Mrs. Ayor agreed to give herself to General Gregory since she was badly desperate to see her husband released from the most feared Blue House prison. Months later, Lang Deng Maluil was released exactly on the help of General Gregory.

But the story did not end there...

Some months later after Lang Deng came home from Blue House prison, his wife Ayor gave birth to a baby. The child was unusually fair-skinned and bore a striking resemblance to Gregory's own children. The baby is purely white just like Gregory's skin. Differentiating the baby from Gregory's children is absolutely impossible. For Lang, the truth was very disturbing to ignore as the baby even cries like Gregory's children as those who knows Gregory's family could attest.

Anger set in. He felt betrayed, humiliated, and powerless. Determined to seek justice, Lang Deng Maluil threatened to take General Gregory to court. “The law knows no wealth and no strong man,” he told friends. “I will fight this.”

Word of the planned lawsuit quickly reached General Gregory. Facing public shame and possible legal consequences, he approached Lang Deng Maluil  privately. According to sources close to the family, General Gregory acted with fear of his reputation and offered Lang Deng Maluil  a deal: drop the case and accept a well-paying government job as compensation.

Faced with few options and the need to provide for his family, Lang Deng Maluil tried to refused, but was convinced by the wife who privately confronted him to accept the job offer as compensation sicne weighting the two position will do something financially rather than a mere 7 cows (a Jieng's customary law for any woman who has committed adultery). Lang agreed to this and he demanded be appointed as MD of NILEPET but Gregory told him that position is impossible because my daughter eyeing to be the Deputy, a situation making hard for Gregory to push for employment of the two officials MD and Deputy MD at NILEPET. So, alternatively, Lang Deng was soon employed in a senior position as the Managing Director for South Sudan Pipeline Corporation, a position that was forcefully taken from a highly qualified young they described as Muony Bor sakit. 

Today, the matter is rarely spoken of in public. But in private conversations, it remains a painful reminder of how power, desperation, and silence can collide and of the cost paid by ordinary people caught in between.

His departure is not only a painful loss to his family but also to everyone whose lives were touched by his wisdom, kindness, and unwavering dedication. He leaves behind a legacy of integrity, compassion, and service that will continue to inspire generations.

May the Almighty grant him eternal peace and comfort his family, relatives, friends, and all those mourning this great loss. May they find strength, courage, and solace during this difficult time.

Though he has departed from this world, his memory, values, and good deeds will remain forever in the hearts of countless people.

May his soul rest in eternal peace.

Former Petroleum Undersecretary Dr. Chol Deng Sells Six-Storey Building Amid Bid to Return to South Sudan's Oil Sector

Former Petroleum Undersecretary Dr. Chol Deng is selling his six-storey building along Juba's Facebook Road as he intensifies efforts to return to a senior position in South Sudan's oil sector, including the top management role at NILEPET.

His renewed political and professional ambitions have sparked criticism from some observers, who have questioned why he continues to pursue influential positions within the petroleum industry instead of seeking opportunities in other areas of public service. Critics have also revived accusations of corruption linked to his previous tenure in office.

Sources in Juba say Dr. Chol recently visited the residence of one of President Salva Kiir's influential aides, where he remained until late at night while seeking support for his appointment to a senior government position.

The same sources say his efforts encountered resistance after he was informed that Minister of Presidential Affairs Africano Mande was standing in the way of his return. He was then advised to challenge Africano Mande for the Minister of Presidential Affairs position as a means of increasing pressure and strengthening his political leverage.

It remains unclear whether the sale of his six-storey building is intended to finance a campaign for the Minister of Presidential Affairs position or to support broader lobbying efforts aimed at securing backing from influential figures within President Kiir's inner circle.

As his campaign to return to government gathers momentum, questions continue to surround his previous record in office. His renewed bid for power is expected to attract greater public scrutiny, with many closely watching whether past corruption accusations will resurface and influence any decision on his possible return to one of the country's most strategic sectors.

As deadly airstrikes continue to hit cities across Russia, the country has reportedly constructed 24 elevated Pantsir-S1 air-defense towers around Moscow to strengthen the capital's defenses against increasingly frequent long-range Ukrainian drone attacks.

By elevating the systems, Russia aims to improve radar coverage and enhance their ability to detect and intercept low-flying drones approaching Moscow.

The Pantsir-S1 air-defense system is equipped with 12 surface-to-air missiles and two 30 mm automatic cannons, enabling it to engage drones, helicopters, cruise missiles, and aircraft at ranges of up to 20 kilometers.

Drone warfare has become one of the defining features of the Russia–Ukraine conflict, with both sides launching thousands of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) every month, prompting major cities to expand their layered air-defense networks.

The U.S. and Israel are considering an unprecedented move: completely sealing off Iran by land.

During their recent White House meeting, Trump and Netanyahu reportedly discussed a land blockade alongside naval pressure and potential strikes to squeeze Tehran. The strategy hinges on choking off all entry and exit points—but there’s a massive catch.

A land blockade requires the full cooperation of Iran’s neighbors, including Iraq, Pakistan, Turkey, and Afghanistan. With deep regional ties to Tehran and zero obligation to Washington, getting all seven bordering nations to simultaneously enforce this blockade seems nearly impossible on paper, let alone in reality.

Could this ambitious blockade ever actually work, or is it just a theoretical threat? Let us know what you think below!

text:
PART ONE

DEAR CITIZENS OF UNITY STATE

BY THE COMMUNITY OF BUL

Subject: Marginalization and the Question of Fair Representation in the Oil Sector

I would like to share a sad history that one of my friends, Parieng, narrated to me yesterday concerning what he described as the continued marginalization of the Bul community and the wider communities of Greater Bahr el Ghazal.

According to him, the ongoing employment opportunities in the oil sector, particularly in GPOC Blocks 1, 2 and 4 and SPOC Blocks 5A and 5B, have largely benefited sons and daughters from the three states of Greater Bahr el Ghazal—Warrap, Lakes and Northern Bahr el Ghazal—as well as one administrative area.

He pointed out that the 45 positions in GPOC and 67 positions in SPOC that became available following the replacement of Petronas positions were, in his view, largely filled by people from those areas. These appointments, he said, included managers, deputy managers, senior heads of sections, superintendents and senior engineers.

This, he argued, represents another chapter in a history of what the Bul community considers nepotism, domination and unequal opportunities in the oil sector.

A QUESTION OF QUALIFICATIONS

Parieng gave me an example involving the son of the former Governor of Lakes State, Riek Tuany Mabor. He said the governor's second son was already serving as a Senior Head in the Production Department at GPOC and was subsequently appointed Deputy Manager of Drilling among the list of 45 employees.

According to Parieng, the individual then brought his cousin to fill his former position in Production. What raised questions, he said, was that the cousin was reportedly a recent graduate holding a Bachelor of Science in Animal Production, a qualification he argued does not directly correspond to the technical requirements of oil production.

He further explained that the governor's son sought to have the individual trained for the position.

However, according to the account, a Chinese manager objected, explaining that the department required professionals such as geologists. The response from the governor's son was reportedly that he would train the individual.

Parieng linked this situation to the subsequent internal arrangement in which Geologist Gabriel Matut was promoted to Senior Head.

ANOTHER QUESTIONABLE APPOINTMENT

He also narrated another case involving a police officer who had previously worked in Immigration and Passports on a database system.

According to him, the officer was included on the list to work in GPOC's Technical Systems (TS) Department as a database officer.

Parieng questioned the suitability of such an appointment, arguing that Technical Systems is a highly specialized technical department requiring a different professional profile from the database work performed within Immigration and Passports.

These examples, he argued, raise broader questions about whether technical positions in the oil sector are being filled according to professional qualifications, experience and merit, or according to connections and influence.

It is also important to remember that GPOC and SPOC are not located in Lakes, Warrap or Northern Bahr el Ghazal. Their operations are based in Greater Unity State, particularly around Bentiu and the oil-producing areas.

“YOUR PEOPLE ARE HOLDING THE COWS’ HORNS WHILE OTHERS ARE MILKING THE COWS”

What struck me most was the way Parieng described the situation facing the Bul community.

He told me:

“Your people who stood firmly with President Salva Kiir are now holding the cows’ horns, while the sons of Bahr el Ghazal are milking the cows.”

The statement was painful, but it was intended to describe what he considers a serious imbalance between sacrifice and reward.

According to him, while the sons and daughters of the Bul community have remained heavily engaged in the restoration of law and order and have continued to defend the government and the country's oil infrastructure, they have not received proportional opportunities within the very oil industry they have helped protect.

A HISTORY OF SACRIFICE

His argument goes beyond the current employment controversy.

He reminded me that the oilfields in Greater Unity have historically depended on the security provided by local communities. He argued that South Sudan's oil reserves, including the oil-producing areas around Mayom and Kaikang in Blocks 4S and 4N, have faced security challenges throughout their history.

During the Sudan period, he said, many people were aware of the relationship between the armed forces associated with President Omar al-Bashir and the forces associated with Paulino Matip. According to his interpretation, that relationship contributed to the security arrangements that made continued oil operations possible in the region.

His point was simple: without the contribution and sacrifice of local sons and daughters, oil production in these areas would have faced enormous difficulties.

The same argument, he said, applies to the period following South Sudan's independence.

THE SACRIFICE OF 2013

He particularly referred to the outbreak of war in 2013, when members of the Bul community chose to defend the government despite facing criticism from sections of the Nuer community.

He recalled how some people were even called “Nuer-wew” because of their decision to stand with the government.

Yet, according to him, the community continued to fight without expecting immediate rewards, while its sons and daughters were deployed to various frontlines to protect the government and maintain security.

From 2013 to the present, he argued, the community has continued to make sacrifices.

His central question, therefore, was:

If the community has consistently provided the security that enables the oil industry to operate, why should its sons and daughters remain excluded from meaningful employment opportunities within that same industry?

MY HEARTFELT RESPONSE TO HIM

I listened to Parieng carefully. His argument was emotional, but it also raised questions that deserve serious consideration.

Communities that contribute to the security and stability of oil-producing areas should not have to beg for recognition. At the same time, employment in the oil sector should be based on qualifications, competence, experience and transparent recruitment processes, regardless of a person's community of origin.

If there are genuine cases of nepotism or unqualified appointments, they should be investigated transparently. If the recruitment process is fair, the institutions responsible should be able to demonstrate that fairness through clear criteria and transparent records.

Ultimately, the issue should not be about replacing one form of domination with another. It should be about ensuring that all South Sudanese citizens, including the communities surrounding the oilfields, have a fair opportunity to participate in the country's economic development.

And as I told my friend:

Successful people always have two things on their lips: silence and a smile. Smile to solve problems, and silence to avoid problems. Master both, and nothing can easily disturb your peace.

The 1983 Attempt to Incorporate Abyei into Bahr el Ghazal and Why It Failed

A Historical Account

During the first quarter of 1983, Mr Abel Alier Kuai de Kut, then Minister of Public Works in the Government of Sudan, and Dr Francis Mading Deng became aware that President Jaafar Mohammed Nimeiri was preparing to promulgate a series of constitutional decrees to reorganise Sudan into several autonomous regional governments.

Believing that the impending constitutional reforms presented an opportunity to resolve Abyei’s administrative status, Mr Abel Alier and Dr Francis Mading Deng sought an audience with President Nimeiri. During the meeting, they proposed that the Abyei Area should be transferred from Kordofan Region to Bahr el Ghazal Region once the new regional arrangements came into effect. According to this account, President Nimeiri expressed his willingness to approve the proposal.

Before any formal decision could be announced, news of the proposal spread and reached several sons of the late Paramount Chief Deng Majok. They strongly opposed the proposed transfer and immediately prepared a petition addressed to President Jaafar Mohammed Nimeiri. The petition was submitted through the Minister for Presidential Affairs, Mr Bahaa El-Din Mohammed Idris.

In their petition, they urged the President not to approve the proposal advanced by Mr Abel Alier and Dr Francis Mading Deng. They argued that when the British colonial administration established Sudan’s administrative boundaries and placed the Abyei Area within Kordofan Province, the arrangement had been made with the consent of their late father, Paramount Chief Deng Majok. They maintained that this was not a unilateral decision imposed solely by the British colonial authorities, as some people believed. They further stated that their father had died while his people remained under the administration of Kordofan and had left no instruction or testament directing that Abyei should one day be transferred to Bahr el Ghazal under any circumstances.

The petition bore the signatures of the following individuals:

1. Zakaria Bol Deng Majok
2. William Deng Majok
3. Hassan Deng Majok
4. Bulabek Deng Majok
5. Alor Deng Majok
6. Kuol Deng Majok
7. Zakaria Atem

Following receipt of the petition, President Nimeiri reportedly reconsidered his earlier position and withdrew his informal commitment to transfer Abyei.

Instead, he appointed a committee chaired by the Under-Secretary of the Ministry of Local Government. The committee included Moulana Martin Majier Gai and Advocate Ashgar Abdallah Shougar, both serving members of the National Assembly. At the insistence of Mr Abel Alier, Dr Francis Mading Deng was also appointed to the committee.

The committee was instructed to organise a referendum in Abyei to determine whether the area should remain within Kordofan Region or be incorporated into Bahr el Ghazal Region. It was decided that voting would be restricted exclusively to the nine Ngok Dinka chiefs.

After completing the necessary preparations, the committee travelled to Abyei and instructed the local administrative authorities to summon the chiefs without delay. All nine chiefs assembled the following day and met with the committee. They were informed that they would be required to vote between two alternatives. The first was for Abyei to remain within Kordofan Region. The second was for Abyei to become part of Bahr el Ghazal Region.

The chiefs were given sufficient time to consider the matter before the vote took place.

On the appointed day, the referendum was conducted openly before a large public gathering. According to this account, seven chiefs voted in favour of Abyei remaining within Kordofan Region, while two voted in favour of its incorporation into Bahr el Ghazal Region.

The committee consequently declared that the option of retaining Abyei within Kordofan Region had secured an overwhelming majority and subsequently submitted its findings to President Jaafar Mohammed Nimeiri.

On the basis of the committee’s report, President Nimeiri issued a Republican Decree confirming that Abyei would remain part of Kordofan Region. Pursuant to that decree, Mr Zakaria Atem was appointed Deputy Governor of Kordofan Region under the Governorship of Major General Al-Fatih Mohammed Bashara.

The decree formed part of the Constitutional Decrees promulgated on 9 July 1983, by which Sudan was reorganised into several autonomous regional governments.

Historical Notes

1. Abel Alier Kuai de Kut is one of the most distinguished statesmen in the history of both Sudan and South Sudan. He served twice as President of the High Executive Council of the Southern Region of Sudan under the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972 and later as Sudan’s Minister of Public Works under President Jaafar Mohammed Nimeiri. He is widely recognised as one of the principal architects and signatories of the Addis Ababa Agreement, which brought the First Sudanese Civil War to an end and established the Southern Regional Government. He also played a leading role in shaping the constitutional framework for regional self-government in Southern Sudan.

2. Dr Francis Mading Deng is an internationally renowned South Sudanese scholar, diplomat and author. He served as Sudan’s Ambassador to the United Nations, Representative of the United Nations Secretary-General on Internally Displaced Persons and later as the first United Nations Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide. He is also recognised internationally for his scholarly work on identity, governance, conflict resolution and Dinka culture.

3. Paramount Chief Deng Majok was the paramount traditional leader of the Ngok Dinka of Abyei during the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium. He played a significant role in the administration of the Abyei Area and maintained close relations with both the colonial authorities and neighbouring communities. His leadership continues to feature prominently in historical discussions concerning Abyei’s administrative status.

4. The Constitutional Decrees of 9 July 1983 dissolved the Southern Regional Government established under the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972 and reorganised Sudan into several autonomous regional governments. These constitutional changes were soon followed by the introduction of the September Laws and the outbreak of the Second Sudanese Civil War under the leadership of Dr John Garang de Mabior and the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement and Army.

5. Editorial Note This document is a translation of the original Arabic source into formal British English. It faithfully reproduces the historical narrative and claims contained in the original text. Certain aspects, particularly the reported referendum involving the nine Ngok Dinka chiefs and its constitutional implications, remain matters of historical interpretation and are not universally documented in the mainstream scholarly literature on the Abyei question. Readers are therefore encouraged to consider this account alongside other primary and secondary historical sources.

Translated from Arabic and edited into formal British English by Chol Michael Maker.

Gogrial Social Media Influencer Akuac Wol and Activist Michael Wetnhialic Clash Over Claims Surrounding the Detention of General Akol Koor Kuc

This post was originally made by Michael Wetnhialic — Friday, 24 July 2026

A public disagreement has emerged between Gogrial social media influencer Akuac Wol and activist Michael Wetnhialic over claims and counterclaims surrounding the continued detention of General Akol Koor Kuc.

The debate, which has unfolded across TikTok, WhatsApp groups, and Facebook, has increasingly focused on the circumstances surrounding General Akol Koor's case, the role of senior officials, and concerns over what Wetnhialic describes as a possible plan to harm or eliminate the detained general Akol Koor according to words from Akuac debate.

In an open letter addressed to General Akech Tong Aleu and Honorable Aleu Ayieny Aleu, Wetnhialic challenged narratives attributed to Akuac Wol, who, according to his account, stated during a TikTok group discussion that General Akol Koor's case was national in nature and that its ultimate resolution rested with President Salva Kiir Mayardit.

Wetnhialic further stated that Akuac Wol had claimed that President Kiir was willing to resolve the matter but that General Akech Tong and Aleu Ayieny had allegedly frustrated the President's efforts. According to Wetnhialic, Akuac Wol also suggested that anyone seeking to advocate for General Akol Koor's release should first consult the two senior officials.

These claims have now triggered a broader public debate, with Wetnhialic questioning why General Akech Tong and Aleu Ayieny would be portrayed as obstacles to a resolution of the case involving their fellow Tonj son and relative.

In his open letter, Wetnhialic urged the two elders to publicly distance themselves from any actions that could negatively affect the life, career, or future of General Akol Koor Kuc.

He warned that continued association of their names and positions with the case could create serious political and historical consequences for them and their families.

«"Do not let this problem, or the case of General Akol Koor, become attached to your honorable names and families. Do not let your brother, General Akol Koor, suffer or die in your hands," Wetnhialic wrote.»

Wetnhialic went further by raising concerns about what he described as a possible "invisible move" by unnamed individuals to use the names and positions of Akech Tong and Aleu Ayieny to harm or eliminate General Akol Koor.

He argued that such an outcome could potentially be used to reinforce longstanding historical narratives surrounding the death of the late William Deng Nhial and claims that he was killed by fellow members of the Tonj Community.

"Maybe there is an invisible move by some people to eliminate Akol Koor Kuc using your names and positions in order to prove that the historical claims that the late William Deng Nhial was killed by his fellow Tonj people are true," Wetnhialic stated.

However, these concerns remain part of Wetnhialic's interpretation of the ongoing debate, and no evidence has been publicly presented in the open letter to substantiate the existence of an organized plan to eliminate General Akol Koor.

Wetnhialic nevertheless called on General Akech Tong and Aleu Ayieny to exercise caution and ensure that their names, positions, and families are not associated with any action that could cause harm to General Akol Koor.

He also appealed to the two officials to forgive any past disagreements they may have had with their brother and to support efforts aimed at finding a peaceful and lasting solution to his case.

Given their senior positions, Wetnhialic argued, the two officials have the influence and capacity to contribute meaningfully toward resolving General Akol Koor's continued house arrest and the broader circumstances surrounding his case.

He further reminded them of General Akol Koor's previous contributions to individuals, communities, and the government, arguing that his past service should be considered in efforts to find a solution to his current predicament.

In conclusion, Wetnhialic cautioned that should anything harmful happen to General Akol Koor while his case remains associated with the names and positions of senior Tonj figures, it could have far-reaching consequences for the individuals involved and could potentially revive sensitive historical narratives within the community.

The public clash between Akuac Wol and Michael Wetnhialic therefore continues to raise questions about who holds responsibility for the circumstances surrounding General Akol Koor Kuc's detention, whether President Kiir has been presented with a genuine opportunity to resolve the case, and whether the ongoing debate is exposing deeper political and community divisions.

For Wetnhialic, the central message is a call for General Akech Tong and Aleu Ayieny to distance themselves from any action that could endanger their brother and to support a peaceful resolution to his case.

"Whatever Akuac Wol says always has its roots and origins," Wetnhialic concluded, urging the two elders to carefully consider the implications of the narratives surrounding General Akol Koor Kuc.

The Community Perspective on the Appointment of Hon. Madhol Chol Thuc as Security Advisor for Warrap State Is in Question

On the night of July 16, 2026, Hon. Madhol Chol Thuc was announced as the new Security Advisor for Warrap State. The appointment has drawn immediate public attention in the Thony area due to allegations linking Madhol Chol to a 2016 incident in Thony in which an anti-tank weapon was used, resulting in the deaths of seven (7) civilians and the subsequent burning of four (4) villages.

To date, no court verdict or official government investigation report on that incident has been published in the public record. The matter, therefore, remains an allegation.

Based on standard community consultation patterns in past conflict areas of Warrap State and Lakes State, the prevailing views expressed by Thony stakeholders can be summarized as follows:

Concern over trust and legitimacy: Many community members, including elders, women's groups, and youth leaders, have expressed concern that the presence of an appointee associated with past violence in Thony could undermine public trust in state security institutions. For survivors and families of the 2016 incident, a visit without prior consultations risks being perceived as insensitive and may reopen trauma.

Given the sensitivity of the allegations and current community sentiment, a direct visit by Hon. Chol to Thony without preparatory engagement would likely be met with resistance, protests, or low community participation.

Security Advisors typically avoid locations where their presence may trigger instability unless the visit is coordinated with local authorities and civil society.

Therefore, it is probable that, in the short term, Hon. Madhol Chol would not undertake an unaccompanied visit to Thony. Any future engagement would require prior groundwork by the state and county leadership. The appointment of Hon. Madhol Chol Thuc presents both a governance challenge and an opportunity for Warrap State.

For Thony, the community's position is clear: security leadership must be accompanied by trust-building, accountability, and respect for victims. Without these steps, the appointment risks deepening divisions rather than restoring peace.

Thony's stability will ultimately be measured not by who holds the title, but by whether civilians feel safer and whether grievances are addressed through dialogue and the rule of law.

text:
Response to Ajou Luol Deng's Defense of Mrs. Arek Aldo

Mr. Ajou Luol Deng's response is notable not for disproving the concerns raised by Watchdog Press, but for attempting to discredit the messenger while avoiding the substance of the allegations.

You stated that "the public is urged to disregard the unfounded allegations leveled against Mrs. Arek Aldo." However, simply labeling allegations as "unfounded" does not make them so. In any democratic society, allegations are answered with facts, evidence, and transparency—not declarations of innocence.

You further argued that "the primary role of a Press Secretary on a presidential mission is to nominate the media personnel who will cover the proceedings" and that "the remuneration of the press team is determined by the Minister or Executive Director." If that is indeed the official procedure, then it should be easy to demonstrate who nominated the journalists, who approved the payments, and how the funds were disbursed. Transparency is the strongest defense against public suspicion.

The assertion that "alleging that funds were solicited by Mrs. Arek Aldo displays a fundamental misunderstanding of governmental procedures" is itself an assumption. Government procedures are only meaningful when they are consistently followed and can be independently verified. Public officials are accountable not only for what the rules say but also for how those rules are implemented.

Your lengthy praise of Mrs. Arek Aldo's achievements—including "the successful launch of the Office of the President's website," "consistent delivery of detailed reporting," and "implementation of watermarked imagery" may speak to her professional accomplishments. Those achievements, however, neither confirm nor refute the allegations under discussion. Competence in one area does not automatically exempt a public official from scrutiny in another.

Likewise, no serious observer has argued that visiting a salon is misconduct. By responding to what you called "the trivial critiques directed at her personal life," you divert attention from the more substantive issues concerning public accountability. Public debate should remain focused on governance, not personal lifestyle.

You also wrote that "the fixation on her UK citizenship is misplaced" and that "dual citizenship... does not constitute evidence of corruption." On this point, you are correct. Citizenship alone is not evidence of wrongdoing, and the public discourse should never confuse nationality with integrity. The real issue is accountability in public office, regardless of one's passport.

Finally, your emphasis on Mrs. Arek Aldo's academic credentials—including degrees from London South Bank University and the University of Delaware—is commendable. Education is an asset, but qualifications are not a substitute for accountability. Public office demands transparency, and neither academic distinction nor professional reputation should place anyone beyond legitimate public scrutiny.

Watchdog Press exists to ask difficult questions on behalf of the public. Journalism is not public relations. It is not the responsibility of the press to protect officials from criticism, but to examine matters of public interest fearlessly and fairly. If any report contains factual inaccuracies, the appropriate response is to provide verifiable evidence correcting those facts—not to dismiss scrutiny as ignorance or misunderstanding.

Public confidence is strengthened when institutions welcome questions instead of treating them as attacks. Accountability is not an insult to government; it is the foundation of good governance.

Watchdog Press – Watching Your Future

Report of Governance and Human Resource Concerns Requiring Attention

Key Concerns:

- It happened that the Governor declined to meet with striking staff, reportedly telling them to “do whatever they want,” instead of engaging in constructive dialogue to resolve the dispute.

- Concerns persist regarding the ongoing irregular and preferential recruitment practices, with proof that relatives and well-connected individuals continue to be recruited outside transparent and competitive processes.

- There are indicators that the Governor intends to promote his Executive Director, Lomini, to the position of Director General.

- It is also discovered that his Executive Assistant, Ms. Nyanchuol Pat, in her 20s, was promoted only last month from Grade 8 to Grade 3 and is now being considered for another rapid promotion to the position of Deputy Director. This has raised concerns among staff regarding fairness, merit, and adherence to the Bank's established promotion procedures.

The Undersecretary at the Ministry of Petroleum, Dr. Santino Ayuel Longar, left Juba for Nairobi without appointing an acting undersecretary before his departure.

After realizing the omission while outside the country, he contacted the Director General for Finance, Hon. Garang Deng Mayath, to prepare an authorization letter assigning the Director General for Planning and Training, Hon. Simon Chuol Martin, to serve as Acting Undersecretary.

This action raises serious concerns about adherence to the ministry's established hierarchy and administrative procedures. It suggests a disregard for institutional governance by treating the ministry as though it were a private entity where acting appointments can be made at personal discretion rather than through official channels.

Given the importance of accountability, respect for due process, and sound institutional leadership, there is an urgent need to replace Dr. Santino Ayuel Longar, also known as Dr. SAL, with a leader who will uphold proper administrative procedures, strengthen institutional governance, and restore confidence in the ministry's operations.

text:
Tonj Community urges President Kiir to grant ‘administrative area’ to address persistent insecurity 

The Greater Tonj Community Union has appealed to President Salva Kiir Mayardit to consider granting Greater Tonj greater autonomy in managing its own security affairs, arguing that the current administrative arrangement has failed to contain recurring violence in the area.

In a letter addressed to the President, the Chairperson of the Executive Committee of the Greater Tonj Community Union, Andrew Kuac Mayol Gai Nyang, said Tonj continues to experience persistent insecurity fueled by widespread possession of illegal firearms among civilians.

He argued that the distance between the Warrap State headquarters in Kuajok and Greater Tonj has made it difficult for authorities to respond swiftly to security incidents, particularly those occurring at night or in remote areas.

The union proposed that Greater Tonj be allowed to govern its own local security matters in order to improve response times and restore stability. It also called for stronger legal powers to be granted to state authorities to enforce law and order and curb armed violence.

In the letter, Andrew reflected on South Sudan's history of armed struggle, saying the country fought for freedom with the expectation that independence would usher in development and improved public services rather than continued internal conflict.

He expressed concern over the continued cycle of communal violence, arguing that repeated peace meetings and reconciliation conferences have yielded limited results as long as illegal firearms remain in civilian hands.

The community leader further urged the national government to intensify efforts to disarm civilians, suggesting that South Sudan could seek technical support from friendly countries if necessary to conduct an effective nationwide disarmament exercise.

Andrew described the proposals as a contribution toward finding a lasting solution to insecurity in Greater Tonj and expressed hope that the government would give them serious consideration.

The letter comes amid continued concerns over recurring intercommunal violence in parts of Warrap State, where cattle-related conflicts and revenge attacks have claimed numerous lives.

text:
The Rebels Within the Government Are More Dangerous Than Those Outside It

After conducting an independent review of the ongoing implementation of the National Social Insurance Fund (NSIF), particularly the proposed management of private-sector employees' social insurance contributions and the growing concerns raised by many affected workers, I have reached a troubling conclusion: some individuals entrusted with serving the government and the public may pose a greater threat to the nation than the armed opposition outside the government.

The greatest danger to any country is not always external. It often comes from within—when public institutions are weakened by individuals who abuse their positions, disregard the law, and place personal interests above the welfare of citizens. Such actions erode public trust, undermine good governance, and threaten the credibility of the government itself.

There is growing public anxiety over whether employees' contributions will be managed transparently, securely, and in full compliance with the law. Many workers fear that their lifelong savings could be exposed to weak governance, inadequate oversight, or even mismanagement if these funds are transferred before the necessary institutional safeguards are fully established and public confidence is earned.

Given the significance of this issue to thousands of private-sector employees and their families, I respectfully urge your investigative team to examine the following matters:

- The current establishment of the NSIF: Whether the formation of the National Social Insurance Fund complies with the provisions of the NSIF Act, 2023, and reflects internationally recognized best practices for the governance and management of social insurance institutions.

- The legality and timing of Ministry of Labour Circular No. 5/2026: Whether the issuance and implementation of this circular are consistent with the NSIF Act, or whether it should only have been issued after all legal and institutional prerequisites required for a statutory body corporate had been fully established.

- The appointment of the NSIF leadership: Whether the current Board of Trustees and Executive Management were recruited through a transparent, competitive, and lawful process; whether they possess the qualifications prescribed under the NSIF Act; and whether any conflicts of interest, favoritism, or other irregularities influenced their appointments.

I further encourage your journalists to examine all publicly available records, official documents, procurement and appointment records, and stakeholder submissions so that the South Sudanese public can receive a balanced, factual, and evidence-based account of this matter.

For my personal safety and to avoid any form of retaliation, I respectfully request that my identity remain strictly confidential and not be disclosed under any circumstances without my prior written consent.

Thank you for your continued commitment to investigative journalism and for keeping the people of South Sudan informed on matters of national importance.

Yours faithfully,

A Concerned Citizen

Being from the Gogrial Community Is Increasingly Becoming a License for Looting Public Resources in South Sudan

People like him will be remembered in the books of accountability once the rule of law is successfully restored in the near future.

text:
News reaching us indicates that the so-called NILEPET Community Development Initiative has donated what it describes as beds, mattresses, and medicines to Juba Teaching Hospital.

This comes at a time when NILEPET staff have not received their medical insurance benefits or treatment allowances since Emmanuel Athiei was appointed Managing Director last year.

It has now become clear, according to allegations circulating from some sources, that officials in J1 are working with the Managing Director to siphon millions of dollars through these schemes.

A source within NILEPET’s General Services (GS) Department, who requested anonymity, said the medical supplies in the truckload were valued at more than US$6 million.

The source further claimed that the Managing Director and his accomplices in J1 have embarked on looting the company without mercy.

The source called on the President to dismiss Athiei and establish an independent committee to investigate the claims before, in the source’s view, the company suffers further financial losses. The source also claimed that Athiei had previously bankrupted ABMC while serving as Director of Finance.
